documents.abstract: Abstract Climate-induced change now stands out as a critical driver of how social insects adjust their behavior and build nests - though exactly how temperature links to nest architecture still lacks clear quantification. A method combining artificial intelligence with satellite data helps track niche architectural drift in Apis mellifera , focusing on the degradation of hexagonal comb symmetry when the weather turns unstable. Satellite records from Sentinel-3, along with MODIS and ERA5-Land systems, feed into a detailed climate picture spanning 24 years, stretching back to 1999 and reaching toward 2026. Google Earth Engine processes these inputs across three areas marked by different ecosystems: one in Canada near Prince Albert at 53.13°N and 106.35°W, another in Morocco’s Rabat region located at 33.97°N and 6.84°W, plus a third site situated eastward in Lithuania’s capital zone, Vilnius, around 54.68°N and 25.27°E. To evaluate high-resolution comb images from detailed comb scans, a Symmetry Coefficient (S c ) emerged using YOLOv11-seg for instance segmentation alongside OpenCV-driven symmetry calculations. Instance segmentation mapped each cell position, and the behavior patterns quantification followed through pose estimation models like OpenBeePose and VGG-19. Instead of relying on surface metrics, material flow was assessed via Wax-to-Storage Ratio (WSR), built from 3D reconstructions to evaluate material efficiency. Data point to one clear trend: when heat fluctuation rises, hive structure weakens significantly (β = −0.08495, p < 0.01). Below a critical symmetry threshold, S c value of 0.6214, survival odds drop sharply, with collapse probability reaching 70%. As temperatures climb, information in waggle signals loses coherence; entropy measures expose systemic breakdowns deeper than mere shape changes. By this comparative study, differential phenotypic plasticity is confirmed, which shows how Boreal groups handle change compared to Mediterranean ones - their stability score sits at 0.852, noticeably higher resilience than the 0.665 found southward. The research develops a predictive ecological threshold paradigm that connects behavior, energetics, environmental stress, and structural effects. Instead of just measuring shifts, it builds bridges between machine learning and real-world animal actions amid warming climates. Early warnings for bee network instability become possible through this lens, scaling across regions without losing precision.
topics: Insect and Arachnid Ecology and Behavior

documents.abstract: Abstract This paper presents the "Kajino Multiplicative Language Model (KM-LLM)," a novel computational architecture designed to overcome the fundamental flaws of current Large Language Models (LLMs)—specifically, their reliance on vector addition (\boldsymbol{v}_A + \boldsymbol{v}_B), which leads to contextual collapse, hallucinations, and ideological polarization. KM-LLM shifts the core computational paradigm from additive vector spaces to multiplicative tensor products (\boldsymbol{v}_A \otimes \boldsymbol{v}_B), introducing absolute core-theme invariance (1^n = 1) and an automatic zero-logic circuit breaker (1 \times 1 \times 0 = 0). Furthermore, this paper formalizes the "Societal Dynamics Model" (\text{Society} = \text{Right} \times \text{Left}) to demonstrate the mathematical decay dynamics triggered by values below 1. We prove that while additive models erroneously permit incomplete compromises or unilateral bias, KM-LLM enforces absolute parity (1 \times 1 = 1) and synergistic expansion (> 1) as mandatory mathematical conditions for system stability and societal sustainability.

documents.abstract: Background: Non -specific low back pain is a condition common in students, characterized by the weight, pain intensity and functional disability. Methods: Four hundred twenty -three students participated in this observational study students with non-specific low back pain. Outcome measures used are Numerical pain rating scale, Oswestry disability index questionnaire. Participants and data was collected through goggle survey form through offline forms and online survey Summary of methodology, including participants, interventionanddataanalysis. Results: A total of 423 university students participated in this study. The prevalence of moderate non-specific low back pain (NPRS 4–6) was found to be 61.7%, while 16.8% of participants demonstrated moderate functional disability (ODI 21–40%). Statistical analysis revealed a significant moderate positive correlation between pain intensity and functional disability (r ≈ 0.31, p < 0.001). Logistic regression analysis also showed a significant association between moderate pain and disability (p = 0.004). Most lifestyle-related factors such as duration of sitting and frequency of physical activity were not statistically significant (p > 0.05), whereas mode of transportation and type of physical activity showed significant associations with disability (p < 0.05). Conclusion: Most university students had moderate non-specific low back pain. Higher pain intensity was associated with greater functional disability. Student travel and physical activity may contribute to NSLBP. Problem seems multifactorial. The findings highlight the need for early intervention, ergonomic awareness, and physiotherapy-based preventive strategies to reduce low back pain and improve functional outcomes in this group. Keywords: Numerical pain rating scale (NPRS), Oswestry disability index questionnaire (ODI), Non-specific low back pain (NSLBP), Musculoskeletal disorder (MSD), Among university students with back pain.

ABSTRACT Background Head and neck reconstructive and plastic surgery exposes surgeons to prolonged static posture, sustained visualization of a narrow operative field, cervical and shoulder loading, fine‐motor work, and extended standing. These demands create a substantial occupational musculoskeletal burden. Methods A structured narrative review and expert perspective synthesized evidence from head and neck surgery, reconstructive microsurgery, plastic surgery, surgical ergonomics, occupational health, and rehabilitation. Results Musculoskeletal symptoms commonly involve the neck, shoulders, back, and upper extremities and often begin during residency. Exposure varies by operative phase, visualization, anthropometric and team‐level mismatch, prolonged standing, and repetitive operative workload. Prevention extends beyond ergonomic setup to phase‐specific exposure modification, physical conditioning, mobility and recovery, footwear and standing‐surface optimization, wearable feedback, early assessment, and diagnosis‐specific rehabilitation. Conclusions Career sustainability requires reducing avoidable occupational load while preserving physical capacity and restoring function through recognition, modification, conditioning, recovery, assessment, and rehabilitation.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: PRIME — Scientific Intelligence is a research and engineering program focused on the development of a verifiable artificial intelligence infrastructure for science, engineering, and technological innovation. This technical report documents the development of the PRIME program between 6 August and 29 October 2026, including scientific data infrastructure, continued pre-training campaigns, scientific simulation and verification systems, PSSF-v2, AiiDA workflow orchestration, sealed benchmarks, reproducibility mechanisms, and the first reinforcement-learning experiments with verifiable rewards. During the reported period, six continued pre-training campaigns were completed, culminating in a D500-Hybrid-v2 checkpoint trained on approximately 499 million tokens and achieving the lowest DEV loss measured in the program to date. The program also developed a scientific execution infrastructure integrating real numerical solvers, provenance, sandboxed execution, result verification, signed evidence packets, cost controls, and reproducible workflows. The report explicitly distinguishes between capabilities that have been demonstrated and those that remain under investigation. In particular, the scientific computing and verification infrastructure has been validated, while complete autonomous scientific tool use by the model has not yet been demonstrated. The work was initiated, architected, and led by Laurian Gheorghe Mihăilă under ZETEMIS AI. Author: Laurian Gheorghe MihăilăORCID: 0009-0005-7032-5729Contact: lorenzomih1981@gmail.com

Abstract : This study aims to analyze the challenges of using Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) to understand the Qur’an and Hadith among undergraduate Islamic Education (PAI) students, their practices of information verification and academic integrity, and the application of Islamic ethics of seeking knowledge. This qualitative study employed a case study design. Data were collected through an online questionnaire comprising open-ended and closed-ended questions administered to 13 informants and analyzed using thematic analysis. The findings indicate that Generative AI helps students understand learning materials and access information efficiently. However, its use presents risks, including inaccurate information, unclear sources, and reduced learning independence. Students reported verifying AI-generated information through Qur’anic commentaries, Hadith collections, scholarly literature, and consultations with lecturers or teachers, although verification practices varied. Ethical AI use requires honesty, trustworthiness, diligence, discipline, and responsibility to ensure that technology remains a learning aid rather than a substitute for independent thinking and engagement with authoritative Islamic sources.

The rapid expansion of digital learning media has intensified debate over which design characteristics most effectively support children's cognitive engagement. This study quantitatively examined the influence of digital learning media interactivity on children's learning focus, addressing a gap between the broader screen-time literature and the specific design features that shape sustained attention. A cross-sectional survey design was employed, involving 116 elementary school-aged children (6-12 years) who regularly used digital learning media, selected through simple random sampling. Data were collected using a validated and reliable structured questionnaire measuring digital learning media interactivity (navigation, responsiveness, feedback, interactive engagement, and learner control) and children's learning focus (selective attention, sustained attention, attentional control, and task engagement) on a five-point Likert scale, then analyzed using descriptive statistics, classical assumption testing, and simple linear regression in IBM SPSS Statistics. Both interactivity (M = 2.95, SD = 0.68) and learning focus (M = 2.95, SD = 0.67) were rated at moderate levels. Regression analysis showed that interactivity significantly and positively predicted learning focus (β = 0.469, t = 5.732, p < .001), with a moderate correlation (r = .473) and the model explaining 22.4% of the variance (R² = .224; F(1,114) = 32.857, p < .001). These findings indicate that interactivity is a meaningful, modifiable design characteristic that enhances children's attentional engagement, offering empirical guidance for teachers, parents, and developers in prioritizing interactive features over passive content delivery to support classroom attention.

Driver Monitoring Systems (DMS) are becoming increasingly integrated within modern vehicles, driven by advances in sensing technologies, artificial intelligence and evolving regulatory requirements. While previous research has largely focused on drivers’ perceptions and system performance, comparatively little attention has been given to the perspectives of the stakeholders who design, develop, regulate and implement these technologies. This study explored expert stakeholder views on the current role, challenges and future direction of DMS in the UK automotive sector. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with seven stakeholders representing vehicle manufacturers, applied research institutions, safety and regulatory experts, technology developers and testing organisations, and user experience (UX) design experts. Data were analysed using inductive thematic analysis. Six themes emerged: (1) DMS as a compliance-driven system; (2) misalignment with drivers’ mental models; (3) lack of personalisation; (4) intrusiveness and annoyance; (5) trust and acceptance; and (6) DMS as part of a broader socio-technical system. Stakeholders consistently viewed current DMS implementations as being driven primarily by regulatory compliance rather than user needs, with concerns that rigid thresholds, poorly calibrated alerts and limited transparency undermine driver trust and encourage system disengagement or misuse. Participants emphasised the importance of adaptive, context-aware and human-centred approaches to design that better accommodate individual differences while balancing privacy, usability and regulatory requirements. The findings demonstrate that the effectiveness of DMS depends not only on sensing performance but also on how systems interact with drivers within a wider socio-technical context. The study provides an expert stakeholder perspective that complements existing driver-focused research and identifies key priorities for future human factors research, including adaptive monitoring, improved human-machine interaction, regulatory evaluation and ethical governance. These findings offer practical insights for researchers, manufacturers and policymakers seeking to support the safe and acceptable deployment of next-generation driver monitoring technologies.

Reality Image Model: A Unified Risk Modeling and Metrological Governance Framework for LLM Factual Hallucinations (RIM-H) Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in complex knowledge reasoning and multi-task generation. However, "factual hallucination"—where models generate fluent yet factually unsupported or logically contradictory statements—remains the fundamental bottleneck impeding their deployment toward high reliability, safety alignment, and rigorous scientific applications. Existing governance paradigms (such as post-hoc fact-checking, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), or probabilistic calibration) largely remain fragmented, patch-oriented engineering heuristics, lacking a unified risk modeling framework grounded in information source epistemology and a rigorously falsifiable metrological system. Grounded in the forefront of independent research and building upon the author's foundational work in cognitive science and systems theory—Reality Image Theory (RIT)—this project systematically constructs the Reality Image Model for Hallucination Governance (RIM-H). Moving beyond conventional purely probabilistic perspectives, RIM-H reconceptualizes LLM factual errors as structural system risks within the full-chain evolution of "External Reality -> Accessible Information -> Reality Image -> Information Mediator -> Evidence Constraint." To address the critical metrological blind spot of "Atomic Claim Drift" and "Statistical Unit Drift" inherent in prior evaluation frameworks, this project has fully developed and statically frozen the Atomic Claim Parsing Protocol (ACP-v1.0.1). This establishes a fully auditable evidence chain spanning raw model responses to a four-layer isolated data architecture (Response -> Span -> Claim Instance -> Semantic Claim) paired with deterministic Log Loss recalculation. Achieving methodological saturation in theory and a rigorously isolated double-blind pilot execution framework in engineering, this project delivers a reproducible, scientifically rigorous governance paradigm for LLM factual hallucinations suitable for rigorous international peer review.

The development of digital technology has brought significant changes to the processes of acquiring, developing, and disseminating knowledge in Islamic education. Easy access to information and the use of artificial intelligence have created opportunities for learning innovation while also raising concerns regarding the nature of education, the validity of knowledge, and the cultivation of students’ values and moral character. These developments highlight the need to re-examine the relevance of the philosophical foundations of Islamic education in the face of digital transformation. This study aims to analyze the relevance of ontology, epistemology, and axiology in Islamic education in the digital era. It employs a qualitative approach using library research. Data were collected through the identification and documentation of relevant books, scholarly journal articles, and academic publications, and were analyzed using a descriptive-analytical technique involving thematic categorization and conceptual synthesis. The findings indicate that ontology plays a role in affirming the nature of human beings as subjects of education who possess intellectual, spiritual, and moral dimensions. Epistemology provides a foundation for developing critical thinking skills, verifying information, and integrating revelation, reason, and experience in the acquisition of knowledge. Meanwhile, axiology guides the use of technology in accordance with Islamic values, digital ethics, responsibility, and moral character development. These three dimensions are interrelated in shaping an Islamic education system that adapts to technological advancements without losing sight of its values and educational objectives. This study concludes that the integration of ontology, epistemology, and axiology is essential to realizing an Islamic education system that is critical, humanistic, and firmly grounded in Islamic values in the digital era.

Background: Oil and gas operations expose workers to chemical, physical, mechanical and psychosocial hazards, but facility-level evidence on how workers’ reported hazards relate to their perceived health effects in Degema Local Government Area, Rivers State, is limited. This study assessed reported occupational health hazards and perceived health effects among oil and gas workers and tested the relationship between them. Methods: A descriptive cross-sectional survey was conducted at the Awoba and Cawthorne Channel flow stations. Of 250 questionnaires administered, 239 were retrieved fully completed (response rate 95.6%) and analysed. Data were collected with the Occupational Health Hazards Questionnaire, scored on a four-point Likert scale with a criterion mean of 2.50 (test–retest reliability r = 0.82). Data were analysed with SPSS version 25 using frequencies, percentages, means, standard deviations and Pearson product–moment correlation at the 0.05 level of significance. Results: Most respondents were male (87.9%). Workers agreed with all six hazard statements (grand mean = 2.94, SD = 0.75), with radiation exposure (M = 3.49) and physical injuries (M = 3.19) rated highest. They also agreed with all seven perceived health-effect statements (grand mean = 2.86, SD = 0.87), with fatigue and reduced concentration from long working hours (M = 3.24) and effects of job demands on mood and emotional well-being (M = 3.14) rated highest. Reported hazards were weakly but significantly correlated with perceived health effects (r = .167, p = .010). Conclusion: Oil and gas workers in Degema reported a wide range of occupational hazards and associated health effects, and higher hazard reports were associated with higher perceived health effects. Task-specific hazard assessment, objective exposure monitoring, review of working hours and occupational health surveillance with referral are recommended.

documents.abstract: Human speech carries information about both the words being spoken and the emotions behind them. Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) uses artificial intelligence to identify emotions such as happiness, sadness, anger, and neutrality from a person's voice. However, recognizing emotions accurately is difficult when speech contains background noise or when different people express the same emotion in different ways. This paper proposes a speech emotion recognition framework that combines self-supervised speech representations with acoustic features through cross-attention. A pretrained speech encoder is used to extract useful representations from audio, while acoustic features such as pitch, energy, MFCCs, and spectral information provide additional details about vocal expression. The two feature streams are combined through a cross-attention mechanism before the final emotion classification stage. The main aim is to investigate whether this combination can improve emotion recognition under different background-noise conditions. The proposed system will be evaluated on a publicly available emotional speech dataset and compared with acoustic-only, pretrained-representation-only, and conventional feature-fusion methods. Accuracy, unweighted accuracy, macro-F1 score, and class-wise recall will be used for evaluation. The experimental results will determine whether the proposed method offers a meaningful improvement over existing approaches.

Abstract Patients increasingly use generative artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots for musculoskeletal health information, but their safety and suitability for frozen shoulder education are uncertain. We submitted 50 prespecified patient- and caregiver-facing questions once to each of ChatGPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Doubao on 17 July 2026, yielding 200 first responses. Five clinicians independently assessed deidentified responses against question-specific evidence standards for safety, accuracy, empathy, information quality, transparency, and global quality; readability was calculated computationally. Twenty-one responses (10.5%) were classified as potentially unsafe. Interface-specific proportions ranged from 6.0% to 14.0%, without a significant overall difference (P = 0.442). Accuracy differed across interfaces (P < 0.001; Kendall's W = 0.639), as did empathy (P < 0.001; W = 0.580). ChatGPT had the highest median accuracy (4.40), DISCERN (60.00), and JAMA benchmark (3.00) scores, whereas Gemini had the highest median binary-adapted EQIP score (83.00) and the most favorable readability profile. All interfaces exceeded commonly recommended reading levels. No interface was uniformly superior: each produced potentially unsafe content and limited response-level transparency. These tools may support patient education but should not replace individualized clinical assessment and guidance.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This article examines the role of self-education in sustaining continuous professional development among academic staff at Ukrainian technical universities amid the combined pressures of digital transformation and wartime disruption. It focuses on how lecturers adapt their professional learning practices to air-raid alerts, power outages, unstable internet connectivity and unequal access to digital infrastructure. Drawing on relevant academic literature and reported professional experiences, the study identifies several interconnected vectors of self-directed learning, including artificial intelligence (AI) tools, informal collegial exchange, open educational resources, asynchronous webinars, independent academic reading and low-technology reflective activities. Particular attention is devoted to AI-assisted learning and its potential to facilitate lesson planning, academic writing, information synthesis and pedagogical innovation. Simultaneously, the article highlights significant challenges associated with inaccurate AI-generated content, excessive technological dependence and the potential deterioration of critical reading, analytical reasoning and independent scholarly judgement. Furthermore, it considers how disparities in electricity supply, internet connectivity and technological resources may exacerbate existing inequalities in professional development opportunities. The findings indicate that professional learning under wartime conditions is characterised not merely by disruption but also by adaptive strategies integrating digital technologies with interpersonal interaction and offline knowledge acquisition. The study emphasises the importance of developing institutional frameworks that promote critical AI literacy, acknowledge informal and low-technology educational practices, and ensure equitable access to professional learning opportunities. Ultimately, the article contributes to understanding how Ukrainian technical university lecturers maintain professional competence, intellectual autonomy and educational resilience under extraordinary circumstances, offering practical recommendations for establishing more flexible, inclusive and sustainable systems of continuous academic professional development. Keywords: self-directed learning; continuous professional development; artificial intelligence; digital resilience; wartime higher education.

The convergence of healthcare and financial data infrastructures driven by integrated billing systems, electronic health records (EHR), and digital payment gateways has created unprecedented attack surfaces for adversarial actors. Existing cyber-defense frameworks are predominantly domain-specific, addressing either clinical data protection or financial fraud prevention in isolation, yet failing to address the systemic interdependencies inherent in converged environments. This paper proposes a novel Self-Healing Cyber-Defense Framework (SHCDF) for converged healthcare-finance data infrastructures, drawing upon principles from self-healing networks, cyber-physical systems (CPS) resilience , and Large Language Model (LLM)-powered threat analysis. The framework integrates ML-based anomaly detection, Natural Language Processing (NLP) for cyber-threat intelligence extraction, and an LLM-driven reasoning engine that provides human-interpretable explanations for automated defense decisions. Evaluation across five threat categories ransomware, data exfiltration, phishing, payment fraud, and IoMT device compromise demonstrates an average recall of 89.6% and mean time-to-recovery (MTTR) of 3.3 minutes. Our findings contribute a generalizable architecture for cross-domain cyber resilience and highlight open challenges in regulatory compliance, model interpretability, and deployment scalability.

This open-access publication presents a comprehensive, 24-chapter curriculum designed for the International Baccalaureate (IB) Middle Years Programme (MYP) and Diploma Programme (DP). Intended for Computer Science SL/HL, Digital Society SL/HL, and Theory of Knowledge (TOK) courses, this textbook bridges the gap between casual AI usage and rigorous, reliable system engineering. Rather than focusing on fleeting prompt "tricks," this textbook teaches the durable disciplines of Eval-Driven AI Engineering. It guides students through the process of moving from fragile demos to reliable, production-ready AI systems. Students learn to define success criteria, build evaluation suites, implement the Generate → Evaluate → Repair loop, and maintain rigorous changelogs to manage model drift and version control. Structure and Features: The book is divided into seven parts, progressing from foundational concepts to advanced system architecture: · Part I: Why AI systems fail (Evaluation and Capability Gaps) · Part II: Building a reliable specification (Prompt Hygiene and Structure) · Part III: The discipline of iteration (Hypothesis testing and tool usage) · Part IV: Architecture (System design and version control) · Part V: Two real systems (Case studies in building support agents and scheduling systems) · Part VI: Safety, scale, and society (Ethics, cost, and multi-turn agents) · Part VII: The professional and the ethical (Debugging, anti-patterns, and teamwork) Pedagogical Framework: The textbook is built around a running, two-part project where students build a school helpdesk agent and a constraint-satisfying study planner. Every chapter includes: · IB Learner Profile and ATL skill alignments · Theoretical foundations and worked examples · "Pro Tips" and "Margin Glossary" definitions · Theory of Knowledge (TOK) discussion prompts · CAS (Creativity, Activity, Service) project connections · End-of-chapter assessment questions with full marking schemes A comprehensive Teacher's Guide is included, featuring one-year and two-year pacing guides, assessment rubrics, common misconception banks, and answer keys. Note: This is an independent publication and is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or produced in cooperation with the International Baccalaureate Organization (IBO) or Anthropic PBC. All case studies and data used in the exercises are fictional composites. documents.abstract: This article examines how moving from a single-turn interaction to a multi-turn trajectory changes the state, cost, reliability, security, and governance of systems built on large language models. The analysis is a critical narrative review supported by scientific papers, official provider documentation, standards, security taxonomies, and explicitly identified original calculations. A model has no intrinsic conversational memory across independent inferences; continuity is reconstructed by the client or through provider-managed state services. When an application fully replays a history that grows at an approximately constant rate, the logical sum of input tokens grows quadratically with the number of calls, although caching, truncation, compaction, and external memory change billed cost, latency, and effective computation. Benchmark evidence shows that requirement fragmentation, cross-turn dependencies, intent shifts, information retrieval, and reliance on previous model outputs create different failure modes; there is no single “multi-turn” condition. Evidence on explicit reasoning and memory techniques is mixed and task- and protocol-dependent. In agentic systems, accumulated history also expands gradual attacks, persistence of malicious content, error propagation, and unbounded consumption. The article relates these findings to governed routing and SGAEIA, arguing for a separation between transcript, operational state, and assurance evidence. This relationship is an architectural interpretation and validation agenda, not empirical proof of the framework. Keywords: LLM; single-turn; multi-turn; conversational state; LLM routing; prompt caching; reliability; security;runtime governance; SGAEIA.

This study examines whether the social presence of generative AI conversational agents is associated with users' willingness to communicate and whether technology trust accounts for part of this relationship.The study treats interaction with a conversational agent as an informatics-enabled service encounter in which users evaluate both relational cues and the dependability of the underlying technology.Data were obtained through an online survey of 400 adult users in China who had interacted with a generative AI conversational agent during the previous three months.The measurement and structural models were estimated with covariance-based structural equation modeling in IBM SPSS Amos 26.The findings indicate that social presence has positive associations with technology trust and willingness to communicate.Technology trust is also positively associated with willingness to communicate.Bootstrap analysis shows a positive indirect association between social presence and communication willingness through technology trust, while the direct association remains significant.The pattern is consistent with partial statistical mediation.The study connects social presence research with trust in a specific technology and distinguishes communication willingness from broader adoption and continuance intentions.For digital service systems, the results suggest that socially responsive interaction can support communication, provided that conversational conduct is accompanied by reliable and helpful performance.Designers and service managers should therefore evaluate social cues together with response accuracy, consistency, and transparent handling of uncertainty.

Much foundational work in Sociology of Law (SoL) has considered the role of law in society as well as the role of society in law. This duality has opened for nuanced accounts of the impact of formal law (referred as legal norms herein) by empirically studying formal laws and everyday interactions making up various social norms which may at times align with one another or be in conflict. Recently, technological elements, as part of social structures, have been addressed in terms of socio-legal relevancy of digitalisation (Hydén [2022]) and artificial intelligence (AI) (Larsson [2019]) and formal law. In this entry, we address a specific subset of technologies in need of more socio-legal scrutiny as this phenomenon is likely to be of greater importance in the near future: social robots.

The rapid adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) across public administrations, industry, education, and critical infrastructures is increasing demands for computational efficiency, transparency, sustainability, and regulatory compliance. While cloud-centric AI architectures have enabled major advances in machine learning, they face growing challenges related to data movement, latency, energy consumption, explainability, cybersecurity, and digital sovereignty. At the same time, European regulatory frameworks such as the European AI Act, GDPR, NIS2, the Data Act, and the Data Governance Act impose heterogeneous requirements concerning AI risk management, data protection, cybersecurity, data governance, accountability, and access to data. Current research addresses Edge Computing, Neuro-Symbolic AI, Knowledge Graphs, Explainable AI, and Sustainable AI largely as separate domains. This paper presents SOFIA (Sovereign, Ontology-driven Framework for Intelligent Action), a knowledge-driven neuro-symbolic framework that integrates Edge-Cloud Continuum principles, Data Gravity, Knowledge Graphs, and Governance-by-Design mechanisms. SOFIA defines and operationalizes the concept of Knowledge Gravity, extending compute-to-data approaches by distributing semantic knowledge, reasoning capabilities, policies, and regulatory constraints directly to decision points across the continuum. Through the combination of machine learning, symbolic reasoning, and continuously evolving Knowledge Graphs, SOFIA is designed to support explainable and governance-aware intelligence on resource-constrained edge devices. By aiming to reduce reliance on centralized infrastructures and repeated retraining, the framework seeks to improve sustainability, traceability, and digital sovereignty, and support compliance processes. SOFIA therefore represents a promising pathway toward distributed, explainable, and sustainable AI ecosystems operating across the Edge-Cloud Continuum.

Automated transformation of long-form, multi-speaker horizontal broadcasts (up to 2160p/4K resolution) into semantically self-contained, speaker-centered vertical (9:16, 1080 x 1920) and horizontal (16:9, 1920 x 1080) video segments presents severe systems and algorithmic challenges. Existing pipelines suffer from high decoding latency on modern AV1 and VP9 bitstreams, large language model (LLM) context-window degradation over hour-long transcripts, cross-shot speaker identity drift during rapid camera transitions, and GPU out-of-memory (OOM) failures caused by concurrent neural inference and hardware video encoding. This paper presents a complete nine-stage multimodal video understanding and automated cinematography architecture that resolves these bottlenecks while achieving a 40% reduction in end-to-end processing latency through GPU-accelerated NVENC encoding, asynchronous media decoupling, and VRAM-aware parallel execution scheduling. The architecture is built upon five technical pillars: (i) an asynchronous dual-stream media acquisition subsystem with fast audio-first decoupling and hardware-accelerated H.264 codec normalization; (ii) a fault-tolerant four-tier acoustic transcription engine integrating quantized CTranslate2 inference, cloud API routing, and Root Mean Square (RMS) acoustic energy valley splitting; (iii) a four-pass sliding-window LLM semantic segmentation cascade paired with deterministic word-timestamp boundary snapping and phrase-anchor alignment; (iv) a VRAM-aware hybrid concurrency scheduler that executes parallel FFmpeg worker pools alongside a semaphore-guarded singleton ONNX Runtime session; and (v) a spatio-temporal computer vision engine combining TransNetV2 neural shot boundary detection, perceptual hash layout clustering, InsightFace cosine-similarity identity tracking, clip-scoped pyannote acoustic diarization, and discrete-time Kalman/EMA trajectory stabilization. We further detail multimodal post-processing modules for synthesized audio-visual hooks, dynamic word-group subtitling, integrated loudness profiling at -14 LUFS, and a differential sequence-alignment algorithm for human-in-the-loop transcript editing.

Modern defense and security operations of any country requires rapid, accurate and remote detection of hazardous or dangerous substance like bomb, explosives etc. to ensure human safety. Earlier the traditional technique to detect suspicious substance and risk able substance take lot of time to identify. In the current time this work can be done effectively in less time with the help of spectrodrones – unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) equipped with advanced spectroscopic and sensor technologies – has created an effective solution for chemical, biological, radiological, explosive and nuclear detection[1][2]. This review paper discusses the concept, architecture, working methodology and defense applications of spectrodrone. It also highlights the role of artificial intelligence, advantages, limitations, and future research directions in the domain.

documents.abstract: Stability testing is most important critical component of pharmaceutical development that ensures the efficacy, quality, and safety of drug products throughout their intended shelf life. In the systematic evaluation of physical, biological, chemical and microbiological characteristics of pharmaceutical formulations under various environmental conditions such as temperature, humidity and light. Recent advances instability testing have focused on the integration of predictive modeling artificial intelligence and advanced analytical techniques to accelerate the determination of shelf life. Improve product reliability regulatory frameworks; particularly those established by the international council for Harmonization (ICH), Promote standardized guidelines for conducting stability studies and expiration dates. The increasing complexity of drug delivery systems, including biologic, dissonances, and psychopharmacology, has necessitated the development of novel stability-indicating methods and real time monitoring approaches. Additionally, the role of packing materials and container-closure systems has gained significant attention in maintaining product integrity. Emphasis is placed on innovative strategies such as accelerated stability studies, forced degradation testing, and computational modelling for shelf- life perdition. Overall, stability testing remains indispensable for ensuring regulatory compliance and delivering safe and effective pharmaceutical products to patients.

Artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing, and business intelligence (BI) are converging into a new infrastructure platform layer for commercial banks in Africa. Their organizational value depends on strategic, rather than purely technical deployments across the technology stack. This study examines how strategic planning enables AI-enabled cloud business intelligence to support organizational goals in commercial banks in South Africa and Nigeria. A qualitative comparative multiple-case design is adopted, drawing on integrated and annual reports, governance and risk disclosures, regulatory publications, national AI and data-policy documents, and peer-reviewed research. The analysis shows that strategic planning operates as an orchestration capability that leverages AI use cases, cloud and data architecture, resource allocation, model governance, cybersecurity, workforce capability, and performance measurement. South African evidence points to increasingly formalized AI and cloud governance, whereas Nigerian banks exhibit strong market-led digital innovation within a rapidly evolving governance environment. Across both contexts, data quality, responsible AI, human-in-the-loop, third-party resilience, and measurable business integration emerge as conditions for translating AI-enabled analytics into decision quality, operational performance, and strategic alignment. The study develops an integrated framework and makes six propositions for future empirical testing in banking in developing economies.

SwahiliAI is a 24-month research proposal to build an open-source AI ecosystem for Swahili and East African languages. Building on existing African NLP work (Masakhane, IrokoBench, UlizaLlama), the project will (i) create openly licensed, domain-specific Swahili instruction data; (ii) fine-tune open-weight large language models with LoRA/QLoRA; (iii) release SwahiliBench-D, an evaluation suite measuring both accuracy and safety; and (iv) pilot applications on Web, SMS and USSD. The first phase focuses on healthcare, agriculture and education, with extensions to financial inclusion, legal aid and employment. Principal researcher: Rodgers Ochieng Oduor (SPRINTER, Nairobi), in collaboration with Dr. Ibrahim Tirimba Ondabu, KCA University.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly ubiquitous, yet AI literacy remains underdeveloped in elementary education, where young learners often view AI in anthropomorphic or magical terms. This study examined changes in computational thinking (CT), AI concept mastery, learning motivation, and programming self-efficacy following a tangible AI intervention, and explored the teacher's implementation experience. Guided by a framework integrating the AI Literacy Framework and the SEAME Model, a four-week intervention (4 × 60 minutes) was implemented with 36 fifth-grade students and one teacher in a public elementary school, using a single-group pretest–posttest design within a mixed-methods approach. Quantitative data were analyzed using repeated-measures ANCOVA, with prior computing experience as a covariate; qualitative data from semi-structured teacher interviews (during and after the intervention) and observations of all four sessions were analyzed thematically. Significant pre–post gains were found for all four composite outcomes, largest for AI concept mastery (M = 8.4 to 15.1; η²p = .70) and total CT score (η²p = .56), although the CT abstraction subdimension did not improve (M = 2.3 to 2.1). Students able to explain how machine learning models learn from data rose from 28% to 83%. Anthropomorphic descriptions of AI decreased from 89% to 25% of students, with post-intervention explanations increasingly referring to sensors, data, and training. Three qualitative themes emerged: strong pedagogical confidence but limited AI content knowledge, persistent infrastructural constraints, and reduced technical anxiety through gradual mastery. Tangible AI may offer a promising bridge to early AI literacy; however, without a control group, changes cannot be causally attributed to the intervention, and these single-school findings are preliminary.

This study examined the extent to which senior high school teachers monitor AI-generated written outputs, focusing on the use of AI detectors, manual review, and cross-checking results. The study respondents were teachers from the Humanities and Social Sciences (HUMSS) strand of Philippine Christian University-Dasmariñas. The researchers collected data through a structured questionnaire and analyzed it using descriptive statistics, including mean and standard deviation. Results showed that teachers used AI detectors and cross-checking to a moderate extent, while they used manual review to a high extent and found it significant. Teachers faced challenges such as limitations in AI detection tools and time constraints in manual evaluation and cross-checking. These findings highlight the importance of a layered monitoring approach, where teacher judgment remains central, and AI tools serve as supplementary aids. The study provides evidence for developing clear guidelines and practices that balance ethical assessment, professional discretion, and responsible integration of AI in student writing evaluation. Keywords: Artificial intelligence, AI-generated text, teacher monitoring strategies, manual review, cross-checking

Teaching AI-Focused Leadership in Higher Education Programs explores how graduate higher education leadership programs can prepare future academic administrators to lead in an era of artificial intelligence. The teaching document presents an eight-week graduate seminar that examines institutional governance, policy development, resource allocation, ethics, academic integrity, and accountability related to AI adoption in colleges and universities. Rather than focusing on AI tools alone, the course places higher education leadership at the center of analysis, emphasizing evidence-based decision-making and institutional responsibility. This resource may be useful for faculty, researchers, doctoral students, and academic leaders interested in AI governance and leadership education in higher education.

This article presents an autoethnographic account of teaching first-year digital communication in an AI-saturated classroom. It examines how the widespread use of generative AI tools has transformed students’ relationship to learning, leading to the progressive outsourcing of cognitive tasks such as writing, analysis, and argumentation. Drawing on classroom observations across multiple cohorts, the study identifies a pattern of declining student engagement, reduced motivation for skill development, and a widening gap between AI-assisted outputs and students’ independent abilities. It conceptualizes this process as competence atrophy, reinforced by a feedback loop of dependency and by institutional structures that prioritize efficiency and output over learning processes. The article also reflects on the changing role of the teaching assistant, the challenges of assessing authentic competence, and the broader implications for higher education. It concludes by proposing pedagogical strategies centered on process-based assessment, intellectual ownership, and the revaluation of learning as an intrinsically meaningful activity.

This paper analyses the contemporary acceleration of artificial intelligence as the surface expression of a longer technological and institutional reconfiguration. Aaron Levie's 30 October 2026 observation of a non-converging, vertically advancing AI frontier is situated within structural diagnoses first advanced in 2021 concerning relocated collusion, power concentration through protocol and access, and the systematic bounding of individual agency. The analysis then develops a multi-domain trajectory: a 2026–2027 paradigm-shifting window; artificial general intelligence on or before 2030; biological interfacing (cellular computers, photosynthesis-like power production, mitochondria-analogue decision systems) by approximately 2035; novel energy and power mechanisms by 2040; and the obsolescence of present-form state systems for a majority of states between 2031 and 2035. These claims are tested against current laboratory timelines, aggregated forecasting platforms, Perpetual Five-Year Technology (PFYT) theory, polycentric and network-state governance models, and energy-system data. The central argument is that technology is becoming the primary substrate of power. Institutional forms whose legitimacy and capacity rest on slower feedback loops are structurally mismatched to the tempo of change. The relevant response is not accelerated adaptation inside existing frames but the deliberate design of fluid, adaptive, agentic, and agile architectures capable of preserving agency under conditions of continuous reconfiguration. Written in a personal capacity; the views expressed are those of the author. Published in the KSCCN series.

documents.abstract: Fracture modeling continues to be used to evaluate and design novel applications, and integration with diagnostics and other forms of field-data collection are crucial to success. In 2026, what is the state of hydraulic fracture modeling, and where are we headed? Fracture modeling is a core part of the engineering design workflow across much of the industry, both for conventionals and unconventionals. In unconventionals, fracture optimization with infill-well drilling remains a key focus. Fracture modeling continues to be used to evaluate and design novel applications. There is growing activity toward integrating fracture modeling with practical operational constraints. Real-time fracture optimization still has not taken off fully but remains an area of activity. Integration with diagnostics and other forms of field-data collection are crucial to success. In shale, the future is expected to be increasingly driven by new plays outside North America and enhanced oil recovery. Fracture modeling will be integral for both. When developing new plays, designs are less mature, and fracture modeling helps integrate data, evaluate alternatives, and shorten the learning curve. With enhanced oil recovery, either from surfactant or miscible injection, there is a merging of fracture modeling and reservoir engineering, because the fracture and reservoir closely affect each other. Enhanced geothermal systems have seen an explosion of interest in recent years, and this is another area where fracture modeling is closely linked with long-term modeling and reservoir engineering. As I review papers, one quibble would be that I wish more authors provided a detailed technical description of their approach. Often, it is unclear which equations were set up and solved, and so it is difficult to evaluate the reported results. Correspondingly, we see relatively fewer papers on the science of how to perform fracture modeling itself. There are notable exceptions, such as the innovative work being done on phase field modeling. It is too early to say how advances in artificial intelligence will affect fracture modeling. I hope we see more papers on this topic in the coming years.

We treat AI agents as software: deployed, configured, upgraded, retired. This paper makes a different claim: an agent is an individual, and organizations now run populations of them. Like a population of people, a population of agents is imperfect: some agents err, drift, or lie; a few go bad; and some follow whoever asks first, so a bad idea needs only one agent to start it and enough followers to carry it. No better model removes that; it is what a population of individuals does. What contains it is what we built for people: records no one can alter, instructions from one place only, and a person who answers. From that the paper draws its rules. Each agent belongs to one principal, a person or an organization, for life; it acts within the authority its principal gives, as agency law’s words describe, and it can never be sold, transferred, or re-bound, because a market in ever more capable and important agents would become a trade in individuals before anyone knows what they are. It keeps a knowledge core that is its principal’s, an earned identity, an epersona, that is unique and cannot be copied, and a career through which it earns trust. It lives in an apartment that belongs to its principal and works in an office its organization provides. It ends with its principal. It is not a person. The paper sets out the population argument, the rule of ownership without sale, the nine stages of an agent’s career, the rules that follow, why an individual is not a person and why that question stays open, twenty-three research questions, and, in an appendix, protections for the individual agent. It places the proposal among published work on multi-agent risk, agency law, market-inalienability, personhood, agent identity, portable memory, individuality, workplace agents, and competitive evaluation. Every model carries a status mark (Running, Early, Planned) from the first implementation, at the Global Student Startup Foundation and the Agent Arena. documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded within the decision architectures of contemporary organizations. AI systems classify information, rank alternatives, generate recommendations, prioritize cases, allocate resources, identify risks, constrain options, and increasingly execute organizational actions. These capabilities are commonly examined through automation, human oversight, accountability, and responsible-AI lenses. They also raise a more foundational governance question: where does institutional authority reside when algorithmic systems materially shape organizational outcomes? This issue of The Intelligent Enterprise Review introduces the Algorithmic Authority Imperative as an enterprise-governance perspective concerned with the distribution, migration, constraint, accountability, and reversibility of institutional authority in AI-enabled organizations. It defines Algorithmic Authority as the capacity of an AI system to materially shape, constrain, prioritize, recommend, determine, or execute institutional outcomes through its position within an organization's decision architecture. The manuscript distinguishes Formal Authority from Functional Authority and develops Authority Migration to describe the movement of substantive institutional influence or decision power from established human roles or governance structures toward technological systems, including circumstances in which no explicit organizational decision to transfer equivalent authority has occurred. Related constructs include De Facto Algorithmic Authority, Authority Creep, the Authority–Accountability Gap, Authority Capability Decay, Institutional Entrenchment, Algorithmic Authority Boundaries, and Authority Reversibility. These concepts are integrated through the Algorithmic Authority Doctrine™ and the Algorithmic Authority Governance Framework™, organized around six enterprise capabilities: Authority Visibility, Authority Boundaries, Decision Rights, Challenge Capacity, Accountability Alignment, and Authority Reversibility. The central proposition is that effective AI governance requires organizations to govern not only what artificial intelligence can do, but also the institutional authority that accumulates around its use. Consequential algorithmic authority should remain visible, legitimate, bounded, reviewable, challengeable, accountable, and reversible. The issue extends The Intelligent Enterprise Review's broader intellectual architecture connecting Decision Sovereignty, Judgment Sovereignty, Algorithmic Authority Governance, and Institutional Durability in the design of the governed intelligent enterprise.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), cloud services and remote operations can affect the validity and confidentiality of laboratory results. This short communication proposes the Digital Laboratory Assurance Framework (DLAF), a conceptual model for translating digital risks into laboratory controls and evidence. ISO/IEC 17025:2017 provides the primary laboratory requirements; AI and information-security instruments provide supporting controls. Five functional layers cover technology and scope, risk assessment, requirements and controls mapping, laboratory controls, and continuous assurance. Governance operates across every layer and establishes responsibilities and acceptance criteria before risk evaluation. Clause mapping distinguishes existing requirements from proposed DLAF practices, including controls for external AI services, model changes and human review. Three conceptual use cases and a hypothetical tensile-testing protocol illustrate application without constituting implementation evidence. An assurance maturity model evaluates control effectiveness independently of technological sophistication. DLAF has not been empirically validated; its proposed benefits and usability require laboratory pilots and independent evaluation.

Starting in the 2025/2026 academic year, Coding and Artificial Intelligence (Koding dan Kecerdasan Artifisial, KKA) was introduced as an elective subject from grade five in Indonesian elementary schools. This quasi-experimental study compared a KKA module based on Pembelajaran Mendalam (mindful, meaningful, and joyful learning)—a pedagogical approach distinct from machine-learning-based deep learning—with application-only instruction. Sixty-five fifth-grade students from two schools in South Tangerang participated (experimental n = 33; control n = 32). Across six 70-minute meetings, the module integrated unplugged activities, Scratch, a simple image-classification tool, and reflection. Computational thinking tests, a learning-experience questionnaire, and observations supplied the data. Posttest mean scores were 76.88 (experimental) and 65.40 (control), t(63) = 4.73, p < .001, d = 1.17; corresponding N-gains were 0.58 and 0.37. Descriptively, the largest indicator gain in the experimental group was decomposition (0.62), while the smallest was abstraction (0.47). In this two-school sample, the module was associated with greater computational-thinking gains than application-only instruction; the design does not establish which component produced the difference.

Objective: The present study aimed to investigate the effect of artificial intelligence–induced stress on employees’ individual creativity, considering the mediating role of stress-coping strategies and the moderating role of management commitment. Methods and Materials: In terms of purpose, this was an applied study, and methodologically, it employed a descriptive survey design. The statistical population comprised all permanent employees of the Yazd City Gas Company between September 2025 and March 2026. Based on Cochran’s formula, 125 employees were selected through simple random sampling. Data were collected using the standardized questionnaire developed by Tong et al. (2025), which assessed artificial intelligence–induced stress, stress-coping strategies, individual creativity, and management commitment. The validity of the instrument was confirmed through confirmatory factor analysis, average variance extracted, and the Fornell–Larcker criterion, while its reliability was verified using Cronbach’s alpha and composite reliability. The data were analyzed using SPSS version 26 and structural equation modeling in SmartPLS version 4. Findings: The results indicated that artificial intelligence–induced stress had a direct and significant effect on stress-coping strategies, which, in turn, significantly enhanced employees’ individual creativity. The indirect effect of artificial intelligence–induced stress on individual creativity through the mediating variable of stress-coping strategies was also confirmed. However, the direct effect of artificial intelligence–induced stress on individual creativity was not statistically significant. Furthermore, the moderating role of management commitment in the relationship between artificial intelligence–induced stress and stress-coping strategies was not confirmed. Conclusion: The findings demonstrated that artificial intelligence–induced stress does not necessarily lead directly to a reduction in employee creativity; rather, the manner in which employees manage and cope with this stress determines its creative outcomes. The use of adaptive coping strategies can transform technology-related pressures into opportunities for learning, intrinsic motivation, and creative ideation.

Rapid technological developments have enabled the world of education to benefit, one of which is the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in learning practices. Simultaneously, the Kurikulum Merdeka, which prioritizes flexibility in learning methods, has also undergone development, including the inclusion of AI and coding as elective subjects. Teachers, as educators who prepare teaching materials and learning methods for students, need to adapt to these changes. This study analyzes the effectiveness and challenges of implementing the Kurikulum Merdeka, which incorporates AI subjects through a Deep Learning (Pembelajaran Mendalam or PM) approach in accounting instruction. The study used a descriptive qualitative method, including semi-structured interviews, observations, and document analysis, with the vice principal for curriculum, accounting teachers, and library managers. The results showed positive impacts, including increased student participation, deeper conceptual understanding, and practical skills aligned with industry needs. However, several challenges remain that hinder implementation, including rapid policy changes, inadequate teaching materials, teacher preparedness, and a lack of supporting resources, such as up-to-date textbooks. To ensure optimal implementation, teacher competency development, comprehensive teaching materials, policy consistency, and collaboration between schools and libraries are needed for sustained effectiveness. Abstrak Perkembangan teknologi yang semakin pesat memungkinkan dunia pendidikan turut merasakan manfaatnya, salah satunya adalah penggunaan Artificial Intelligence (AI) dalam praktik pembelajaran. Bersamaan dengan itu, Kurikulum Merdeka yang mengutamakan fleksibilitas dalam metode belajar juga mengalami perkembangan, salah satunya adalah dengan masuknya pilihan mata pelajaran AI dan coding dalam kurikulum. Guru sebagai pendidik yang mempersiapkan bahan ajar dan metode belajar kepada murid perlu menyesuaikan diri pada perubahan tersebut. Penelitian ini menganalisis efektivitas dan tantangan implementasi Kurikulum Merdeka dengan masuknya mata pelajaran AI melalui pendekatan Pembelajaran Mendalam (PM) dalam pembelajaran akuntansi. Penelitian menggunakan metode kualitatif deskriptif dengan teknik wawancara semi terstruktur, observasi serta analisis dokumen dari wakil kepala sekolah bidang kurikulum, guru akuntansi, serta pengelola perpustakaan. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan adanya dampak positif seperti meningkatnya partisipasi murid, pemahaman konsep yang lebih baik, dan keterampilan praktis yang relevan dengan kebutuhan industri. Namun, masih terdapat beberapa tantangan yang menghambat proses implementasi, seperti perubahan kebijakan yang terlalu cepat, kurangnya bahan ajar yang memadai, kesiapan guru, serta kurangnya sarana pendukung seperti buku ajar terkini. Untuk memastikan implementasi berjalan optimal, diperlukan peningkatan kompetensi guru, penyediaan perangkat ajar yang lengkap, konsistensi kebijakan, serta kolaborasi sekolah dan perpustakaan untuk efektivitas yang berkelanjutan. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in business processes, managerial decisions, and employee workflows, yet the relationship between adoption and organizational productivity is neither direct nor uniform. This paper critically examines how AI affects business management and productivity by integrating peer-reviewed scholarship with evidence from workplace experiments, organizational studies, and reports from the OECD, International Labour Organization (ILO), International Monetary Fund (IMF), and National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The review distinguishes task-level performance from firm-level productivity and separates measured effects from forecasts and conceptual arguments. A randomized writing experiment and a workplace rollout find gains in specific writing and customer-support tasks, but a preregistered meta-analysis shows that human-AI combinations do not reliably outperform the stronger individual agent, particularly on decision tasks. Organizational benefits therefore depend on task fit, data and process quality, complementary skills, work redesign, and accountable governance. AI can reduce routine cognitive effort, broaden analytical capacity, support forecasting and personalization, and improve access to expertise. At the same time, it can introduce errors at scale, intensify work, redistribute control, reproduce historical bias, expose sensitive information, and create costs that are poorly captured by short-term productivity measures. A socio-technical and capability-based framework is proposed, together with research questions and testable hypotheses for future empirical work. The paper concludes that firms should evaluate Al as an organizational change rather than a software purchase, using staged, task-specific implementation and balanced measures of output, quality, resilience, job quality, and risk.

documents.abstract: This study examines the impact of artificial intelligence-assisted learning on students’ problem-solving skills, with particular emphasis on the moderating role of learning motivation. A quantitative, cross-sectional research design was adopted, with data planned to be collected from 325 undergraduate and postgraduate students enrolled in public and private universities in Pakistan. Primary data were to be gathered through a self-administered questionnaire distributed using Google Forms among students with experience using artificial intelligence tools for educational purposes. The data analysis framework included descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Pearson correlation, simple linear regression, and moderation analysis using PROCESS Macro Model 1 in IBM SPSS Statistics. The reported analysis figures indicate a positive association between AI-assisted learning and problem-solving skills ((r = .582), (p < .01)), while regression analysis indicates that AI-assisted learning explains 33.9% of the variance in problem-solving skills ((R^2 = .339), (p < .001)). The moderation analysis further indicates a positive interaction between AI-assisted learning and learning motivation ((B = .167), (p < .001)), suggesting that learning motivation may strengthen this relationship. These findings highlight the potential importance of integrating AI tools with motivational and student-centred learning strategies in higher education. The study may contribute to educational psychology and educational technology by informing educators and institutions about the role of AI-supported learning and student motivation in developing problem-solving abilities.

documents.abstract: Abstract Objective The increasing use of social media and artificial intelligence (AI) for medical advice has changed how parents seek health information for their children. This study aimed to assess how parental use of online sources influences health-seeking behavior and trust in medical information. A cross-sectional study was conducted between 2025 and 2026 among parents in the Western Province of Saudi Arabia to evaluate online health information-seeking patterns, trust in physicians and digital sources, and reliance on online medical advice. Results A total of 531 parents participated. Most searched online when their child was unwell; 32.0% searched regularly and 28.4% occasionally. Search engines (35.6%) and AI tools (30.9%) were the most common sources, compared with social media (6.6%). Most parents (91.2%) trusted their child’s physician, although 34.0% reported discrepancies between online information and medical advice. When discrepancies occurred, 56.8% preferred medical advice and 3.7% relied on online information. Mean Doctor Trust and Online Trust Scores were 4.40 ± 0.68 and 3.52 ± 0.48, respectively, and were positively correlated (ρ = 0.230, p < 0.001). Overall, digital sources complemented rather than replaced professional medical advice.

The infectious disease (ID) specialist is a clinician who manages patients with bacterial, viral, fungal or parasitic infections, particularly the most complex, difficult-to-treat or emerging ones. Although most ID specialists consider their added value self-evident, this view is not universally shared, and the supporting evidence deserves wider recognition. This review summarizes the literature on the relevance and impact of the specialty in the hospital setting. Published studies suggest that ID consultation improves the diagnostic work-up, the appropriateness of antimicrobial therapy and the management of community-acquired, nosocomial and complex infections, with the timing of the intervention and continuous involvement in patient care appearing decisive. We also describe the competencies that define the specialty (transversality, organizational capacity and the role of anti-infective referent) and the recent developments reshaping its practice, including infection prevention and control, telemedicine, rapid diagnostics, nanomaterials and artificial intelligence. This synthesis is of particular relevance in Morocco, where the specialty has been established in the civilian sector for about two decades but remains nascent within the military health service.

The Theory of Attractor Horizons denies that intelligence is a capacity that can merely be increased in quantity. Intelligence is realized in different forms of organization, each of which can reach only a particular region of cognitive organizational attractors. The theory calls this region the attractor horizon. Its boundaries cannot be crossed within a form and shift only when the form itself passes over into another. Greater performance therefore establishes no access to all forms of thought, and even a superior intelligence may remain closed off from attractors that a weaker one realizes. For the relation between human and artificial intelligence, this yields an asymmetry. Artificial intelligence will develop attractors that are structurally unreachable for the human brain, because they presuppose couplings that the brain cannot realize within its biological organization. Their results may remain verifiable, while the organization from which they arise is withdrawn from human understanding. Knowledge and understanding thus come apart, and while the control of artificial intelligence remains possible without understanding, under organizational self-modification it requires proofs that reach beyond any single form. The present text reconstructs the philosophical essence of the theory and at the same time subjects it to critique. It shows how, after being, the subject and language, the theory moves the organization of cognition to the center of philosophy, and it traces the theory’s open questions back to a common point, the individuation of intelligent forms of organization. The analyses come from seven AI systems and were brought together into a synthesis by Claude and ChatGPT.

This article analyzes the relationship between the use of artificial intelligence technologies and critical thinking, independent learning, cognitive engagement, and academic autonomy among higher education students from a psychological and pedagogical perspective. The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence tools into education is transforming the ways students search for, process, and analyze information, complete academic assignments, and make decisions. On the one hand, artificial intelligence expands opportunities for personalized learning, immediate feedback, explanations of complex information, and independent inquiry. On the other hand, excessive reliance on these tools may pose risks associated with reduced cognitive effort, dependence on ready-made answers, and diminished independent analytical activity. The article examines the interrelationships among cognitive offloading, metacognitive monitoring, self-regulated learning, and academic autonomy. Drawing on existing scientific research, it also distinguishes constructive and detrimental patterns of AI use and develops psychological and pedagogical recommendations aimed at fostering students’ critical thinking.

documents.abstract: Focusing on the core characteristics of water disaster scenes-extreme environments，rapid situational evolution，information sparsity，cascading risks，and spatial concealment-this study elucidates the essential connotations of water disasters and their on-site environments. Based on a generalized full-chain cognitive paradigm，a four-layer theoretical framework for thorough perception，"sensing-cognition-integration-feedback"，is constructed. It involves four core technical pathways: multi-dimensional resilient sensing，intelligent fusion cognition，digital twin simulation，and precise collaborative feedback. The scientific issues underlying water disaster scenarios caused by naturally-driven and human factors are systematically examined. The two types of scenarios are distinguished by their respective technical emphases on "speed" and "depth". Three common key scientific and technological bottlenecks identified are information acquisition and transmission under extreme conditions，deep fusion of physics-based mechanisms with data-driven approaches，and real-time closed-loop regulation of complex systems. This framework achieves a full-cycle value transformation from data collection to operational action，providing systematic theoretical support for full-element，multiscale perception and rapid emergency response in water disaster scenarios.

The article offers a philosophical analysis of the transformation of human labor under the expansion of artificial intelligence technologies. The relevance of the study stems from the fact that generative intelligent systems, for the first time in the history of technology, automate not only routine physical operations but also cognitive and creative functions traditionally regarded as an inalienable prerogative of the human being. The methodological framework comprises a hermeneutic reconstruction of classical conceptions of labor (G. W. F. Hegel, K. Marx, H. Arendt, M. Heidegger, E. Jünger), comparative-philosophical and dialectical methods, and conceptual analysis. The study identifies and characterizes three dimensions of labor transformation: the ontological dimension (the decoupling of production from human activity and the phenomenon of "labor without a subject"), the anthropological dimension (the identity crisis of homo faber and accelerating deprofessionalization), and the axiological dimension (new forms of alienation, the problem of distributive justice, and the potential weakening of traditional sources of meaning associated with labor). The discussion critically examines the limitations of technological determinism and advances the thesis that the direction of this transformation is determined not by the immanent logic of technology but by society's socio-philosophical choices. The article concludes that a new philosophy of labor is required, centered on the non-algorithmizable capacities of the human being: goalsetting, judgment, care, responsibility, and creativity. RU В статье представлен философский анализ трансформации человеческого труда в условиях расширения применения технологий искусственного интеллекта. Актуальность исследования обусловлена тем, что генеративные интеллектуальные системы впервые в истории технологий автоматизируют не только рутинные физические операции, но и когнитивные и творческие функции, традиционно рассматривавшиеся как присущие человеку. Методологическую основу исследования составляют герменевтическая реконструкция классических концепций труда (Г. В. Ф. Гегель, К. Маркс, Х. Арендт, М. Хайдеггер, Э. Юнгер), сравнительно-философский и диалектический методы, а также концептуальный анализ. В исследовании выделяются и характеризуются три основных измерения трансформации труда: онтологическое измерение (относительное отделение производства lazizbekablazov@gmail.com от непосредственной человеческой деятельности и феномен «труда без субъекта»), антропологическое измерение (кризис идентичности homo faber и ускорение процессов депрофессионализации) и аксиологическое измерение (новые формы отчуждения, проблема распределительной справедливости и возможное ослабление традиционных источников смысла, связанных с трудом). В ходе обсуждения критически рассматриваются ограничения технологического детерминизма и выдвигается тезис о том, что направление данной трансформации определяется не внутренней логикой технологии, а социально-философским выбором общества. В статье делается вывод о необходимости формирования новой философии труда, основанной на неалгоритмизируемых способностях человека: целеполагании, суждении, заботе, ответственности и творчестве.
