documents.abstract: This chapter employs computer-mediated communication as a thematic lens to illuminate how transnational migrants navigate connectivity and agency within digital environments. We focus on relational communication engaged in by transnational migrants, especially for unprivileged ones, thereby uncovering the intersecting dynamics that shape their experiences of social inclusion and exclusion. Here, “relation” extends beyond mere migrant-media interactions but encompasses: (1) transnational social connections; (2) digital hybridity within networks; and (3) negotiated identities bridging cultures. Though continuously impacted by technological and geopolitical shifts, migrants negotiate the tensions of displacement, constructing agency across diverse digital media. Future scholarship should critically address the escalating influence of non-human agents that fundamentally reshape these relational dynamics, particularly generative artificial intelligence.

Judul: Trends, Effectiveness, and Urgency of Adaptive Scaffolding in Digital and Web-Based Geometry Learning Multimedia: A Systematic Literature Review (2022–2026) Ringkasan Singkat: Artikel Systematic Literature Review (SLR) ini disusun berdasarkan protokol PRISMA 2020 untuk memetakan tren, efektivitas, serta urgensi penerapan adaptive scaffolding (dukungan perancah adaptif) dalam multimedia pembelajaran geometri digital dan berbasis web. Melalui skrining terhadap 344 dokumen Scopus unik rentang tahun 2022–2026, studi ini mengidentifikasi 12 studi utama (core studies) dan 14 studi kontekstual dari pendidikan matematika. Poin-Poin Kunci & Temuan Utama: Tipologi Dukungan: Sebagian besar penelitian berfokus pada perancah konseptual (visualisasi 3D/animasi) dan prosedural, sementara perancah metakognitif/strategis serta mekanisme pembongkaran dukungan secara bertahap (fading mechanism) masih sangat terbatas. Efektivitas Pembelajaran: Efektivitas perancah adaptif sangat bergantung pada respons sistem terhadap kesalahan siswa, kemampuan spasial awal, dan gaya pemrosesan kognitif—sejalan dengan expertise reversal effect dalam Cognitive Load Theory. Celah Teknologi: Walaupun teknologi interaktif berkembang pesat (seperti VR/AR, intelligent tutoring, dan AI generatif), penelitian yang secara khusus mengintegrasikan arsitektur web-native 3D (seperti WebGL/Three.js) dengan mesin adaptif masih sangat minim. Agenda Penelitian 2026–2030: Artikel ini merumuskan 4 prioritas riset mendatang, yaitu: Pengembang sistem adaptif berbasis web (web-native adaptive engines). Perintah AI generatif yang terarah (rule-guarded generative-AI prompts). Desain eksperimen longitudinal dengan mekanisme fading. Evaluasi pembelajaran yang berkeadilan dan berfokus pada inklusivitas (equity-oriented evaluation).

documents.abstract: This study aims to map the discussion of Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence (TAI) in internal auditing research. A qualitative approach using a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) guided by PRISMA 2020 was employed to examine articles indexed in Scopus within the 2016–2026 search window. A total of 44 articles met the inclusion criteria, all of which were published between 2020 and 2026. The data were analyzed descriptively and thematically, focusing on publication trends, AI technologies, audit domains, and TAI dimensions. The reviewed literature indicates that AI is increasingly discussed as a tool to support anomaly and fraud detection. Meanwhile, discussions of trustworthiness primarily focus on accountability and governance (65.9% of articles) and transparency and explainability (59.1%), with considerably less attention given to fairness and ethics (15.9%) and human oversight (9.1%). These findings suggest that the literature remains fragmented between technical performance and non-technical governance aspects. This study provides an integrated mapping of AI technologies, audit domains, and TAI dimensions, distinguishes between auditing with AI and auditing of AI, and proposes a research agenda toward continuous AI assurance. As a review of published studies, the findings reflect the current state of the literature rather.

documents.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has created new challenges for academic integrity in higher education. Although previous studies have primarily examined academic misconduct among university students, less attention has been paid to college students and the factors that may mitigate their intentions to engage in such misconduct. Accordingly, this study examines the relationships between four factors and college students’ intentions to violate academic integrity in the context of AI use. A survey was conducted with 358 college students in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. The data were analyzed using Cronbach’s alpha, exploratory factor analysis (EFA), Pearson’s correlation analysis, and multiple linear regression. The results indicate that perceived risk, perceived behavioral control, and attitudes toward academic misconduct are significantly and negatively associated with misconduct intentions, whereas subjective norms are not statistically significant. Perceived risk exhibits the strongest negative association with misconduct intentions (β = −0.514). This study contributes empirical evidence from a college student population and extends the application of the theory of planned behavior (TPB) by incorporating perceived risk alongside its original components. The findings suggest that educational institutions should establish clearer academic integrity policies, communicate the consequences of misconduct, and provide students with practical guidance on the acceptable use of AI.

Purpose This study explores how university students use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) across various disciplines, including STEM, Business, Education Futures, Clinical & Health Sciences (CHS), Creative and Allied Health & Human Performance (AHHP). It aims to identify discipline-based perspectives, perceived benefits, ethical boundaries and the support needs required for responsible use of GenAI tools. Design/methodology/approach A survey was conducted approximately two years after the widespread use of GenAI, by which time participants were expected to be familiar with its use. Students were categorised based on their discipline, English fluency, mode of learning and level of study. Their responses were analysed to compare usage patterns, satisfaction levels and ethical considerations across disciplines. Findings The results highlight that student perspectives on GenAI tools are discipline-dependent. STEM and Education Futures showed the highest acceptance, while CHS and Business students were more cautious and sceptical about accuracy and ethical issues. Non-native English speakers rated GenAI tools more favourably as aids for writing and comprehension. Novice users expressed enthusiasm, while expert users showed dissatisfaction due to errors and false information. Research limitations/implications The study relied on self-reported perceptions and represents a single institutional context. Broader investigations are recommended, with a particular focus on equity groups such as students with disabilities, low-SES students and remote learners. Practical implications Different approaches were suggested for integrating GenAI into learning. STEM students favoured comparative tasks; CHS recommended support for diagnostic reasoning; Allied Health preferred role-playing simulations; Education Futures highlighted lesson planning; and Business students suggested case-based and productivity uses. Originality/value The study provides cross-disciplinary analyses of GenAI use by students and proposes approaches for ethical and discipline-specific integration into university curricula.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) capability has become a critical organizational resource for enhancing innovation and sustaining competitiveness in increasingly digital business environments. Despite growing interest in AI adoption, limited empirical evidence explains how AI capability translates into employees' innovative work behavior (IWB), particularly in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), where innovation depends heavily on human capital rather than formal research and development. Drawing on the Ability–Motivation–Opportunity (AMO) Theory, this study develops and tests a model in which Psychological Empowerment (PE) and Knowledge Sharing Behavior (KSB) mediate the relationship between Artificial Intelligence Capability (AIC) and Innovative Work Behavior. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted among 350 Indonesian SME employees with experience using AI-enabled digital technologies. The proposed model was analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results demonstrate that AI capability significantly enhances innovative work behavior both directly and indirectly by strengthening employees' psychological empowerment and encouraging knowledge-sharing behavior. The mediation analysis further confirms that empowered employees who actively exchange knowledge are more likely to transform AI-enabled resources into innovative workplace practices. These findings extend AMO Theory by conceptualizing AI capability as an organizational ability that creates employee innovation through complementary motivational and opportunity mechanisms. This study contributes to the emerging literature on AI-enabled organizational innovation by integrating technological, psychological, and behavioral perspectives into a unified framework within the SME context. From a managerial perspective, the findings suggest that investments in AI technologies should be accompanied by initiatives that cultivate employee empowerment and collaborative knowledge exchange to maximize innovation outcomes and improve organizational competitiveness.

Student feedback is central to English as a Foreign Language (EFL) instruction; however, scaling qualitative interpretation while preserving contextual meaning remains a methodological challenge. This study proposes the T-CADS-LLMs framework, a qualitative text topic analysis framework integrated into an Agent Skill. Rather than treating large language models as autonomous coders, the framework positions them as context organizers constrained by corpus evidence and human verification. Its feasibility was evaluated using interview data from 27 students across two majors in university EFL courses. Across ten course grouped analytical units, 46 manually generated topics were compared with 63 Skill-based topics and 42 GPT-based topics using Topic Coverage, Weighted Coverage, MATS, WMATS, and qualitative analyses of matched topics. Codex+Skill consistently outperformed the Bare-model in descriptive mean scores for coverage (0.672 vs. 0.502), weighted coverage (0.721 vs. 0.600), MATS (0.778 vs. 0.700), and WMATS (0.816 vs. 0.772). Nevertheless, both workflows showed limited ability to capture relational and identity related meanings, performing substantially below human analysis. These findings provide initial evidence for the feasibility and traceability of the framework within a specific EFL context, while further validation with larger and more diverse datasets remains necessary.

Organizational theories usually treat participation as actor-bound: the actors whose interests are at stake are expected to occupy the interactions through which outcomes are produced. Agentic artificial intelligence and other autonomous representatives weaken that correspondence. This conceptual article develops a theory of delegated participation, defined as the authorized transfer of communicative, evaluative, coordinative, or exchange-related participation from a principal to a representative. The argument moves beyond treating participation delegation as merely another agency relationship. When representatives operate on multiple sides of an exchange, they form an interaction system that can persist without direct principal participation, reshape the alternatives reaching principals, and separate participation from accountability. The model identifies activity conditions, capability–structure alignment, and authorization as antecedents; bilateral representation and interaction displacement as mechanisms; and symbolic concentration and representative-centered organizing as organizational consequences. The framework contributes by challenging the actor-bound conception of participation, identifying bilateral representation as a discontinuity in organizing, and explaining why declining principal participation may coexist with persistent principal accountability and increasingly consequential symbolic appearances. The article concludes with managerial implications and an empirical research agenda focused on recruitment, procurement, customer service, and AI-mediated negotiation.

Global policy mandates accelerate transport electrification, yet the environmental benefits of smart charging (SC) and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) remain uncertain and context dependent. This systematic review synthesizes 88 peer-reviewed studies (2011 - 2025), retrieved through a dual-branch search combining sociotechnical adoption literature (Search A, n = 57) with environmental and grid-performance evidence (Search B, n = 31), to identify conditions under which SC and V2G are reported to deliver or fail to deliver sustainability benefits. The study proposes an integrated sociotechnical framework structured as a two-tier architecture: a parsimonious primary framework (seven constructs, six directed pathways) supported by classifiable evidence, and a hypothesis-generating extension for recurrent but unvalidated constructs. The framework is explicitly calibration-derived and requires future empirical validation. Evidence indicates that behavioral determinants are associated with participation intentions but are linked to actual participation only when structural conditions are present. Model-based evidence indicates that SC and V2G may increase emissions in high-carbon grids, demonstrating that these technologies are not inherently sustainable without aligned policy and energy system conditions. Four candidate contextual conditions including grid carbon intensity, infrastructure density, market maturity, and prior experience are recurrently identified as potentially conditioning deployment and emissions outcomes. These contributions shift policy discourse from overcoming user resistance to composing enabling conditions, offering context-dependent recommendations for deployment associated with measurable environmental benefits rather than unintended emission increases.

documents.abstract: Introduction: Burnout among nurses is an important occupational health concern because persistent physical and emotional exhaustion may compromise work performance, quality of care, and patient safety. Workload, work-related stress, and shift work are frequently considered important occupational determinants of burnout, particularly among nurses working in high-intensity clinical units. This study aimed to examine the associations of workload, work stress, and shift work with burnout among nurses at Jaury Jusuf Putera Academic Hospital, Makassar, Indonesia. Research Methodology: A quantitative cross-sectional study was conducted among 36 nurses working in the Intensive Care Unit and Emergency Department. Total sampling was applied. Data were collected using structured questionnaires and analyzed using the Chi-square test. Crude odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were derived from the reported 2×2 contingency tables to describe the magnitude of associations. Results: Of the 36 nurses, 19 (52.8%) experienced high burnout. High workload was not significantly associated with burnout (OR = 2.45; 95% CI: 0.64–9.37; p = 0.187). Nurses with moderate work stress had substantially higher odds of high burnout than those with mild stress (OR = 9.00; 95% CI: 1.97–41.08; p = 0.003). Shift work was also significantly associated with burnout (p = 0.047); nurses classified in the high-shift category had lower crude odds of high burnout than those in the low-shift category (OR = 0.25; 95% CI: 0.06–1.01). Conclusion: Work stress and shift work were significantly associated with burnout, whereas workload was not. Hospital management should prioritize stress-management strategies, adequate recovery periods, and evidence-based shift scheduling to reduce occupational burnout and support nurses’ well-being and service quality.

Background: The workplace represents an ideal setting for cardiometabolic prevention, enabling early identification of workers with overweight and metabolic alterations and the implementation of structured lifestyle interventions. In this context, collaboration between the occupational physician and the dietitian integrates risk assessment with a personalized nutritional pathway, aimed at improving adherence to the Mediterranean diet and daily habits. Case presentation: Within a workplace health promotion study conducted in a university hospital in Rome, two clinical cases are described. The first patient, a 65-year-old woman with overweight, abdominal obesity, impaired fasting glucose, and low adherence to the Mediterranean diet, showed at three-month follow-up a reduction in body weight from 78 to 75 kg, waist circumference from 99 to 97 cm, normalization of blood glucose, and improved dietary and physical activity habits. The second patient, a 61-year-old man with hypercholesterolemia and impaired fasting glucose, initially presented with a weight of 86.7 kg and a waist circumference of 97.5 cm; after three months, weight decreased to 81.5 kg and waist circumference to 93.5 cm, with normalization of altered metabolic parameters. Results: In both cases, the most relevant outcome was a substantial shift in dietary habits toward a Mediterranean pattern, associated with an overall improvement in lifestyle, with benefits in both anthropometric and metabolic parameters. Conclusion: These cases suggest that an integrated pathway combining occupational health surveillance and nutritional counseling, embedded within workplace health services, may represent an effective, sustainable, and reproducible approach for preventing non-communicable chronic diseases, strengthening the role of the workplace as a key setting for health promotion.

This study examines the ethics of using artificial intelligence in audience viewing data analysis for television channels and digital platforms, given the growing reliance of media organizations on algorithmic systems to understand audience behavior and guide content production. The study aimed to identify the major ethical risks and violations associated with these applications. A survey approach was adopted, and in-depth interviews were conducted with a sample of media experts and software engineers. The findings revealed that collecting audience data without informed consent constitutes a major ethical concern. The results also showed that AI algorithms can re-identify individuals even after anonymization by linking different data variables. In addition, algorithmic bias and the manipulation of public trends through fake accounts may distort audience preferences. Participants emphasized the need for ethical review and oversight mechanisms to ensure transparency, privacy protection, and accountability in AI-driven media practices.

documents.abstract: This study examines whether Moroccan Law No. 95.17 on Arbitration and Conventional Mediation can accommodate electronic means in the resolution of business disputes, at a time when state justice is rapidly going digital following the entry into force of Law No. 03.23 amending the Code of Criminal Procedure and Law No. 58.25 on Civil Procedure, and when international standards are shifting after UNCITRAL adopted new texts on electronic arbitral awards in July 2026 and the EU Artificial Intelligence Act classified AI systems used in alternative dispute resolution as high-risk. It argues that the Moroccan legislator adopted an approach of “permission without regulation”: the law allows arbitration and mediation agreements to be concluded by electronic message, pleadings to be filed electronically, and awards to be rendered on an electronic medium, yet it leaves unregulated remote hearings, the notion of the “original” of an electronic award and its deposit, the proof of electronic notification, and the use of artificial intelligence. Using an analytical method supported by comparison with UNCITRAL instruments, institutional arbitration rules, and UAE and EU legislation, the study concludes that the effectiveness of these tools depends on an integrated reading of Law No. 95.17 together with Law No. 43.20 on trust services and Law No. 09.08 on personal data protection. It proposes targeted legislative and regulatory reforms, notably codifying remote hearings with explicit safeguards, enabling electronic deposit of awards and settlement agreements, setting rules on the use of AI, and considering accession to the Singapore Convention on Mediation. Keywords: Electronic arbitration; Conventional mediation; Law No. 95.17; Trust services; Remote hearings; Artificial intelligence; Digital justice; Business disputes.

This study aims to reveal the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies on shaping news-sharing behavior among university students on social media platforms. It focuses on the level of trust in news content presented through algorithms. The study employed a survey methodology, using a questionnaire to collect data from a random sample of 200 university students. The results showed that AI technologies have become an influential element in organizing the digital news environment through recommendation systems and content ranking based on audience engagement indicators. The results indicated that news-sharing decisions are increasingly influenced by the news's reach and associated engagement levels, with the majority of respondents exhibiting caution before sharing news. The study also revealed a relative awareness of the risks associated with algorithms, such as reduced media diversity and the potential for misinformation.

documents.abstract: Personalized drug therapy aims to improve treatment efficacy and safety by considering individual genetic, molecular, physiological, and clinical characteristics. Biomarkers support patient stratification, treatment selection, dose optimization, response monitoring, and prediction of adverse drug reactions. This critical narrative review evaluates current advances, clinical applications, translational challenges, research gaps, and future perspectives related to biomarkers in personalized drug therapy. Pharmacogenomic biomarkers help explain interindividual differences in drug pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, efficacy, and toxicity. In addition, multi-omics, immune, imaging, liquid-biopsy, and digital biomarkers are expanding the scope of individualized pharmacotherapy. These approaches have shown important clinical utility in oncology and are increasingly being explored across cardiovascular, neurological, immunemediated, metabolic, and other therapeutic areas. However, clinical translation remains constrained by inadequate analytical and clinical validation, assay variability, limited representation of diverse populations, difficulties in interpreting rare genetic variants, uncertain clinical utility, high testing costs, ethical concerns, and limited integration into routine healthcare. Biomarkers can support a shift from empirical prescribing toward more precise and individualized drug therapy. Their successful implementation will require prospective clinical validation, standardized testing, diverse population datasets, regulatory harmonization, integration of multiomics and clinical information, and evidence of real-world clinical and economic benefit. A combined approach incorporating pharmacogenomics, therapeutic drug monitoring, modelinformed precision dosing, and artificial intelligence may provide a more comprehensive foundation for individualized drug therapy.

Language learning history is the personal narrative of an individual's journey in acquiring a second language, including motivations, strategies, challenges, and contextual factors. This study explores Jamal’s language learning history as an English lecturer at Parwan University to understand the factors that contributed to his English proficiency. A qualitative case study design was employed, utilizing a language learning history questionnaire, VARK inventory, oral and written assessments, and a semi-structured interview. The findings of this study indicated that Jamal's success was driven by strong intrinsic motivation rooted in his interest in English movies and fiction. His learning was shaped by social factors like limited interaction with foreigners and restricted technology access, as well as cultural challenges with informal English. His kinesthetic and auditory learning preferences emerged as key strengths. He demonstrated advanced oral and written skills but exhibited developmental weaknesses such as filler words in speech and minor cohesion issues in writing. The study concluded that Jamal is an upper-intermediate to advanced English user who succeeded through personal initiative and strategic effort. His journey highlights the importance of intrinsic motivation, awareness of learning styles, authentic materials, and targeted feedback for Afghan learners in similar contexts.

Large language models do not encounter users, projects, institutions, or environments directly. Each provider invocation presents the model with a bounded construction assembled from governing policy, retrieved evidence, runtime observations, persistent memory, tools and capability descriptions, selected history, the current user request, and vendor or base-system instruction. These source classes form PROMTHUS: Policy, Retrieval, Observations, Memory, Tools, History, User request, System instruction. PROMTHUS is an inventory, not an authority hierarchy or serialization order. Its sequence serves a mnemonic and Promethean construction; it does not imply that Policy is universally supreme or that later classes possess lower standing. PROMTHUS names the principal materials from which an invocation context is compiled. To promthe an invocation is to subject those materials to constitutional context compilation: governed discovery, authentication, semantic finding, independently derived consequence analysis, contest, adjudication, authorized transformation, budget closure, provider realization, effect authorization, and evidentiary sealing. This paper proposes constitutional context compilation as a typed authorization, adjudication, and transformation layer between context sources and inference. The compiler governs what may count as context, what may govern inference, what may be disclosed, how admitted context may be transformed, what may cross a provider boundary, which consequences may follow, and what must remain auditable afterward. The architecture defines the minimum contract required of a Constitutional Kernel capable of governing context compilation. Such a kernel must provide an explicit and non-extensible bootstrap basis, identity-bearing root law, governed discovery obligations, authorized amendment, court jurisdiction, non-self-ratification, typed judgment, structurally triggered contest, review and appeal, refusal semantics, independent effect authorization, and witness. The paper distinguishes a presupposed Grundnorm Basis from a positive, executable Root Constitution written in Deterministic Semantic Compiler (DSC) form. DSC coding means that law is expressed as explicit, canonically serializable, content-identified rules that execute deterministically over admitted structured predicates, rather than as prose whose application depends on interpretation at the moment of use. The Grundnorm Basis identifies the genesis custody and initial standing that any finite constitutional order must presuppose. It is fixed at genesis and cannot later be enlarged by declaration. The Root Constitution makes operational successor law deterministic over admitted structured predicates, inspectable, content-identified, testable, auditable, and mutable only through authorized amendment. Context-specific law derives from that root. Discovery profiles, calibration profiles, conflict-detection profiles, independence profiles, domain canonicalization profiles, consequence tiers, court procedures, provider-adapter contracts, and effect boundaries all receive standing from law outside the discretion they constrain. Any profile whose declarations bound the scope of scrutiny must be identity-bearing, evidence-class-typed, and adjudicated before use. Identity itself is layered to avoid a bootstrap circularity. A primitive, exclusion-free Constitutional Canonical Form (CCaF), bound into the genesis recognition machinery, identifies constitutional objects; adjudicated domain profiles govern application material. Every identity is permanently typed by the layer under which it was computed, and relations across layers are typed correspondences rather than collapsible equivalences. Completeness of governance is made checkable rather than asserted. A discretion census over the declared schema and transition registry enumerates every mechanism able to affect identity, authority, admission, scope, scrutiny, conflict detection, transformation, realization, effect permission, or evidentiary claims, and each censused locus must bind to an audit row or a proven reduction to one. Classifiers do not become lawmakers; their outputs become receipted findings subject to calibration, conservative consequence computation, independent contest, judicial review, appeal, and refusal. The context compiler executes admitted judgments. The Context Intermediate Representation is the identity-bearing product of that governed process, not its source of authority. The architecture distinguishes six principal failures: context loss, containment loss, authority loss, representation loss, realization loss, and receipt loss. It defines three layers of context identity over two canonicalization layers, strict partial-order precedence, inter-court conflict law, scrutiny-profile adjudication, cross-layer correspondence, governing projections, delegation contracts, autonomous-loop review, availability protections against stay flooding, privacy-preserving receipts, two-phase budget closure, staged conformance, and measurable governance cost. Its general constitutional proposition is: Every mechanism that determines whether another mechanism is scrutinized must itself be governed by authority external to the discretion it constrains. The paper audits the architecture against that proposition by enumerating its discretionary loci, the power held at each locus, the external governor, the evidentiary record, and the failure emitted when governance is absent. The discretion census supplies the enumeration procedure, so the audit's completeness claim rests on a declared schema rather than on architectural omniscience. The architecture does not prove truth, model understanding, obedience, classifier completeness, contest independence beyond available evidence, profile completeness beyond available evidence, or remote-provider honesty. This paper specifies a narrower conditional assurance claim: a conforming realization may establish, relative to its declared capability surface and evidence, that context was assembled under explicit machine-governance rules, adjudicated through authorized procedures, realized according to an admitted adapter contract, and bound to evidence sufficient for later inspection. The paper itself is a proposal and proof-obligation map; it supplies no implementation-conformance verdict. A constitutional context layer could unify memory, retrieval, personalization, policy, capability exposure, delegation, and long-running automation within one systems discipline. It would also make durable computational agency portable across replaceable inference providers---where the user or another legitimate custodian actually holds the registry, amendment authority, and receipts on which such portability depends.

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT The automatic assessment of handwritten answers in low‐resource Indic scripts is a difficult problem because of the complexity of the orthographic ligatures, the variability of the writers, limited availability of annotated resources, and the error propagation from handwritten text recognition (HTR) to the grading modules. In this paper, we aim to address these challenges by introducing an end‐to‐end framework that combines Text Region Detection, sequential HTR, and Generative AI (GenAI) using Large Language Models (LLMs) for Explainable Multilingual Answer Assessment. The proposed framework was evaluated using a Telugu handwritten character dataset containing diverse character forms, including basic characters, vowel modifiers, compound characters, vattu combinations, and diacritics. A conditional Generative Adversarial Network (cGAN) was employed to generate synthetic Telugu character samples and increase handwriting diversity, which were integrated with the original training images. The framework was assessed using Character Recognition Accuracy (CRA), Word Recognition Accuracy (WRA), precision, recall, and F1‐score to evaluate recognition effectiveness and generalization. The proposed system carries out pre‐processing of document images and region awareness for Text Detection in document images using Character Region Awareness for Text Detection (CRAFT) based on non‐heuristic segmentation to avoid explicit character segmentation. Detected handwritten text regions are then recognized and transcribed to text by using a Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network with Connectionist Temporal Classification (CRNN‐CTC). An LLM‐based GenAI refinement module corrects accented characters, checks for word spelling errors, and corrects errors based on the context while maintaining the student's original meaning and intent and without spurious corrections. Next, with the text structured with the correct answer key, each is processed by a carefully designed text understanding module to locate the key concepts, to create a semantic map, and finally, using the rubric‐aware scoring from contextual embeddings, to identify answer points. The signals produce an explainable assessment tuple which includes awarded marks, concept coverage metrics, missing criteria and personalized LLM‐generated diagnostic feedback. The framework integrates computational intelligence through deep visual representation learning, generative augmentation, and knowledge‐aware semantic evaluation for robust recognition of complex handwritten Indic scripts. The proposed system achieves high transcription fidelity, strong linguistic refinement in multilingual Indic corpora of Hindi, Telugu, and Kannada, while also achieving high human–AI evaluation agreement, making it a scalable automated academic evaluation system.

Perkembangan e-commerce yang pesat mendorong integrasi Artificial Intelligence (AI) untuk meningkatkan pengalaman belanja konsumen. Namun, mekanisme psikologis internal yang menjembatani interaksi AI dengan keputusan pembelian aktual masih belum konsisten dan sering kali mengabaikan keseimbangan antara jalur kognitif dan afektif. Penelitian kuantitatif eksplanatori ini bertujuan untuk mengembangkan dan menguji model dual-path consumer engagement berbasis AI dalam mendorong keputusan pembelian konsumen e-commerce di Indonesia. Data dikumpulkan melalui kuesioner dari 196 responden pengguna e-commerce , lalu dianalisis menggunakan metode Structural Equation Modeling-Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS). Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa AI berpengaruh langsung yang positif dan signifikan terhadap keputusan pembelian konsumen. Selain itu, AI terbukti memiliki kontribusi yang sangat besar dalam membentuk Cognitive Engagement dan Affective Engagement. Model struktural membuktikan bahwa Cognitive Engagement berperan secara positif sebagai variabel pemoderasi yang memperkuat pengaruh AI terhadap keputusan pembelian. Sebaliknya, Affective Engagement tidak bertindak sebagai pemoderasi melainkan menjadi pendorong langsung (direct driver) yang masif bagi keputusan pembelian. Kesimpulannya, penyedia platform e-commerce harus menyeimbangkan efisiensi fitur kognitif berbasis AI dengan pendekatan emosional guna mengunci loyalitas dan keputusan transaksi konsumen digital secara berkelanjutan.

The Flexible Image Transport System (FITS) is a widely adopted standard for storing, exchanging, and analysing astronomical data. Developed in 1979, formally described in 1981, and endorsed by the International Astronomical Union in 1982, FITS combines multidimensional numerical arrays and tabular data with structured metadata that support scientific interpretation. This narrative review examines the historical development and internal architecture of FITS, including Header/Data Units, data types, and header keywords relevant to photometric calibration, coordinate transformations, and observational provenance. It compares FITS with consumer and general-purpose raster formats, distinguishing the preservation of numerical values from the retention of astronomical metadata and calibration context. Representative applications in major space missions and observatory pipelines illustrate the role of FITS in managing images, spectra, and time-series data. The review also discusses the preparation of FITS-based data for artificial intelligence and machine learning, including calibration, quality filtering, normalization, and metadata integration. Particular attention is given to the distinction between archival data containers and the numerical arrays or tensors used by computational models. FITS provides a well-established foundation for reproducible astronomical analysis, although scientific validity and model performance depend on data quality, calibration, preprocessing, and methodological choices rather than file format alone. The review offers an educational foundation for students and researchers developing computational methods for astronomical classification and physical parameter estimation.

Determining whether a genetic variant is harmful is one of the central open problems in clinical genomics. Sequencing throughput has grown far faster than the human expertise available to interpret its output, and the result is a growing backlog of variants that carry no actionable clinical label. Roughly two out of every five variants reported by clinical diagnostic tests in protein-coding regions are recorded as Variants of Uncertain Significance, and only a small fraction of these are ever reclassified. This survey reviews the machine learning methods developed for variant effect prediction over the past decade, organised into six families: alignment and conservation scores, feature-engineered ensemble classifiers, protein language models, DNA language models, graph neural network approaches, and structure- informed or phenotype-conditioned predictors. For each family we examine the representation used, the supervision signal, the treatment of class imbalance, the evaluation protocol, and the computational cost. Three recurring weaknesses emerge. First, most published systems are formulated as binary classifiers over confidently labelled variants and discard the uncertain class entirely, which removes the majority of clinically difficult cases from evaluation. Second, random row- level train and test splitting remains common, permitting gene-level memorisation and inflating reported accuracy. Third, the highest-performing recent systems depend on very large foundation models or on multi-source biomedical knowledge graphs whose compute requirements place them out of reach of ordinary laboratory hardware. We then present GenoHybrid-VEP, a proposed framework designed against these findings. It couples a one-dimensional convolutional encoder over a 101 base-pair genomic context window, a dense encoder over clinical and population biomarkers, and a graph convolutional encoder over variant co-occurrence relations, fusing the three into a single latent representation for three-way classification. Variants of Uncertain Significance are retained as a first-class label, training uses gene-grouped splitting with balanced class weighting, and epistemic uncertainty is quantified through Monte Carlo dropout so that low- confidence predictions can be flagged rather than silently reported. The framework is described here as an architectural proposal; empirical validation is reserved for subsequent work.

documents.abstract: This paper presents an educational tool designed to support active learning in engineering education by guiding and promoting the ethical use of artificial intelligence. The proposal targets undergraduate engineering students and is grounded in a real classroom context structured through university extension activities and project-based learning. The tool integrates artificial intelligence as a pedagogical support mechanism, assisting students in organizing technical reasoning, structuring disciplinary content, and communicating results, while preserving the central role of critical thinking and instructor mediation. The instructional design includes clearly defined learning activities, intended learning outcomes, assessment criteria, and ethical guidelines for the responsible use of artificial intelligence, to facilitate adoption and adaptation by other educators. Intended learning outcomes encompass the ability to analyze engineering concepts, synthesize technical information from diverse sources, and communicate effectively through written and audiovisual artifacts. The paper describes the instructional structure, activity sequence, and supporting materials required for implementation, thereby promoting straightforward replication in similar educational contexts. Classroom observations indicate increased student engagement, improved organization of technical content, and more reflective use of digital tools when artificial intelligence is explicitly framed as a learning support rather than as an autonomous content generator. The contribution emphasizes the practical, replicable nature of the proposed tool and invites the engineering education community to adapt, apply, and further evaluate the approach across diverse instructional settings.

documents.abstract: While the function of university libraries is central to teaching, learning and research, they are often hindered in their function by a lack of integration of aesthetic quality and functional efficiency. Several papers have researched aesthetics and functionality separately but rarely together; hence the need for this research. This paper looks at the connection between aesthetics and functionality in some University libraries in Southwest Nigeria. The mixed-methods approach used was a combination of a structured questionnaire that was completed by 644 library users (students and staff) from six universities, direct observation and semi-structured interviews. Descriptive statistics, a composite perception index and inferential analysis (correlation, independent-samples t-test, one-way ANOVA and regression analysis) were used for data analysis. The Cronbach's Alpha value of the perception scale (0.902) was used to validate the reliability of the scale. The regression analysis showed that academic achievement, well-being, and library learning engagement were significantly predicted by the perception of the library (p < 0.01), and there was a strong relationship between the library features and academic achievement, well-being, and learning engagement (β = 0.684, R² = 0.468, p < 0.01). The study concludes that a university library in Southwest Nigeria is functional but has been underutilised in terms of its aesthetic and experiential potentials and suggests design considerations such as flexible spatial planning, ergonomic furniture, better lighting, good ICT infrastructure, and culturally responsive detailing towards designing comparable library projects.

Abstract The rapid advancement of Financial Technology (FinTech) has significantly transformed the structure and functioning of the Indian financial system. The growth of digital payment platforms, mobile banking, artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing and data-driven financial services has changed the way individuals and businesses access and use financial services. In India, digital payments have emerged as an important component of financial transformation, while Artificial Intelligence is increasingly being used for fraud detection, credit assessment, customer service, risk management and personalised financial services.This study examines the role of FinTech in transforming the Indian financial system, with particular emphasis on digital payments and Artificial Intelligence. The study proposes an analytical framework linking FinTech adoption, digital payment usage, AI-enabled financial services, consumer trust, cybersecurity and financial inclusion. A structured questionnaire can be used to collect primary data from users of digital financial services. The proposed study may employ descriptive statistics, correlation and regression analysis to examine relationships among the major variables. The paper also discusses opportunities and challenges associated with technology-driven financial transformation, including cybersecurity risks, digital fraud, data privacy, technological barriers and the digital divide.

Abstract Artificial Intelligence, also known as AI, is transforming the modern workplace by making employees more efficient at analyzing, creating, admin and decision making. Modern AI systems have the capability of handling vast amounts of data, identifying patterns, creating content, summarizing information, offering recommendations, and conversing in natural language. These capabilities are driving organizations to adopt a model where technology and employees work together rather than the traditional automation model. But, human-AI collaboration doesn't just happen by simply introducing an AI tool. It relies on employee capability, trust, transparency, organizational preparedness, governance of data, security of privacy, and defined humans' role. This paper explores the concept of human–AI collaboration and its impact on productivity, decision-making, creativity, learning, customer service, and organizational performance. It creates a conceptual framework that unfolds around five related dimensions: AI capability, human capability, interaction and trust, organizational readiness, and responsible AI governance. The paper also evaluates the challenges that include job transformation, algorithmic bias, lack of explainability, privacy and security concerns, skill deficits, change resistance, and overreliance on AI. A human-in-the-loop approach is suggested, to enable the level of human involvement to correspond to the risk of the task. The paper argues that the best model for the workplace is not one that pits man against machine, but one that uses AI to drive computational power and leaves judgment, creativity, context, ethics, interpersonal responsibility, and accountability to the humans. The activity encompassed discussions on AI's role in decision-making, its impact on productivity, the future of work, responsible AI, and the skills required to work alongside AI.

documents.abstract: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into academic workflows has significantly transformed the landscape of scholarly writing. This paper explores the application of AI tools in structuring academic papers, with a specific focus on how generative AI and large language models (LLMs) can assist researchers in organizing complex data and adhering to rigorous publishing standards. By analyzing the traditional challenges associated with academic structuring—such as maintaining logical flow, formatting citations, and organizing the IMRaD (Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion) framework—this paper demonstrates how AI can be utilized as an assistive technology to enhance efficiency and coherence. Furthermore, the paper critically examines the limitations and ethical considerations of AI-assisted writing, including the risks of fabricated citations (hallucinations) and the importance of preserving human critical thinking. Ultimately, this paper argues that while AI offers powerful structural scaffolding for academic manuscripts, it must be deployed as a supportive tool rather than a replacement for human intellectual rigor and academic integrity.

Artificial Intelligence has really transformed areas like healthcare, legal services, education, finance, and business. But its quick spread also brings persistent tech troubles, mainly the confusing issue of AI mistakes, errors, and misinformation. Large Language Models (LLMs) can handle all sorts of tasks, from text creation and code writing to answering questions and summarizing info. Still, despite their big achievements, LLMs sometimes spout incorrect stuff – factually wrong or made-up content – which is called "hallucination." This paper dives deep into AI failures, showing how they differ based on errors in logic, generated fiction presented confidently, and correct data being misinterpreted. It looks at why AI systems act overly sure of themselves, how messy training data messes up, and ideas for fixing this like boosted retrieval methods, cleaner training data, and humans checking the work. What stands out is that these glitches aren't just random tech snafus. Instead, they're a design quirk of big AI language models. Fixing them demands teamwork from folks in various fields, not just developers. So, while there are big issues, figuring out ways to collaborate could make these systems way more reliable in the future.

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) has disrupted assessment in higher education and accelerated an existing cycle of performativity. Institutional policies demand the demonstration of independent authorship in assessed work, yet AI models enable students to mimic independent work that is ultimately not their own. Some institutions and educators have responded by using AI text detection technologies, although their use appears contested and uneven. Within this environment, AI humanizers have emerged. These internet-based services alter AI-generated text to evade human and technological detection. Although humanizers have attracted increasing public attention, there is a dearth of scholarly literature on the subject. This paper presents the first exploratory, systematic investigation of AI humanizer websites, framed through Goffman’s sociological account of dramaturgy. Using a systematic search and custom rubric, we catalogue 55 humanizer sites, assessing their performance of identity and conducting an in-depth multimodal critical discourse analysis (MCDA) of a purposive sample of three sites. Findings reveal that humanizers appeal to students as consumers through multiple strategies, performing legitimacy work by recontextualizing their service as a rational and defensible response to surveillance, engaging in mystification by presenting their products as proprietary, advanced technologies, and drawing on symbols of authority and trustworthiness (such as university logos) to build user confidence. We argue that humanizer services form a node in an ongoing feedback loop, in which assessment requires performances of legitimacy, and those performances create demand for technologies that enable them.

Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly used by university students to compare alternatives, obtain recommendations, and support academic decisions. This study examines whether objective AI literacy and perceived reliability can predict student trust in generative AI-assisted decision-making. A cross-sectional online survey yielded 406 responses. After eligibility screening, 310 respondents met the inclusion criteria, and 280 respondents who passed the attention check served as the primary analysis sample. AI literacy was measured using 12 multiple-choice questions, while perceived reliability and user trust were measured on a five-point scale. Item analysis supported the removal of two negatively worded items that had low item-total correlations. Multiple linear regression with HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors showed that the model explained 52.1% of the variance in user trust. Perceived reliability was the dominant predictor (standardized beta = 0.704; p < 0.001), whereas AI literacy provided a smaller positive contribution (standardized beta = 0.101; p = 0.022). The AI literacy coefficient was non-significant in a sensitivity analysis that retained all eligible respondents. These findings indicate that student trust primarily depends on the assessment that generative AI outputs are accurate, consistent, relevant, and reliable. Higher education institutions need to integrate AI literacy education with verification practices so that students are capable of assessing system reliability before using AI recommendations.

documents.abstract: The chapter looks on how AI systems and other advanced IT solutions can be used in connection to human modelling activities. AI has been used in this sense more than 30 years, earlier with focus on the use of symbolic AI. Various approaches have lately been using existing data for doing modelling on a higher abstraction level, with a focus in recent years on the use of a generative AI. More traditional machine learning also plays a greater role in support of human modelling. In model-driven engineering, the focus was later on generating code from models. Now, code can, to a larger extent, be generated from existing code using generative AI. On the other hand, other usages of models for analysis and design are still areas where the human must be clearly in the loop, due to that e.g. analysis and requirements models must still be developed through social construction. In our neuro-conceptualisation research, we analyse biometric data to eventually develop neuro-adaptive modelling systems for areas where human modelling is important.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence has become a dominant technology in digital business and has greatly changed how businesses interact with customers. Digital businesses increasingly use AI-based technologies to deliver convenient, personalized services. Such technologies include Chatbots, virtual assistants, recommendation systems, personalized advertisements, automated customer support, and AI-powered search. These developments have changed customer expectations and affected their willingness to use and continue using digital services. Therefore, businesses operating in a thriving digital environment must understand AI from the customer’s perspective. The study covers a broad spectrum of AI dimensions, including personalization, efficiency, ease of use, responsiveness, reliability, service quality, security, and privacy. These factors are expected to influence customers’ behavioral intentions, including buying behavior, usage, purchasing patterns, and recommending AI-enabled digital services. The study also investigates “Customer experience and Customer engagement as mediators” to understand how AI impacts customers’ behavioral responses. The study has adopted a quantitative research approach. The study collects primary data through a questionnaire from customers with experience using AI-enabled digital business services. The study measures customers’ perceptions and behavioral intentions using a five-point Likert scale. The study uses descriptive statistics, correlation, and regression to examine the relationships among AI, Customer experience, Customer engagement, and behavioral intention. The findings provide a clearer view of AI’s effect on consumer behavior, helping digital businesses enhance convenience, personalization, Customer engagement & experience; address privacy & security concerns; build customer trust; and encourage continued use of AI-enabled digital services.

Abstract Safe and effective gene delivery remains a central challenge for therapeutic applications. While non-viral and viral vectors have enabled substantial progress, their reliance on non-human components often triggers immune responses, limiting their use in chronic treatments. Here, we developed DeepDelivery, an artificial intelligence-driven platform to repurpose human proteins for mRNA delivery. An unbiased screening of the human proteome nominated 512 candidates, with experimental validation confirming that 80% of top-ranked hits form mRNA-encapsulating particles and mediate efficient functional delivery in human cells without provoking detectable inflammation. Notably, multiple tripartite motif (TRIM) family proteins, typically linked to antiviral responses, exhibited strong assembly and delivery activity. Quantitative analysis and interpretation of the model revealed structural domains that govern nanocage formation, enabling domain-guided engineering of TRIM25 variants with enhanced function. Our work establishes a generalizable framework for discovering human-derived delivery vehicles and provides a path toward programmable, non-immunogenic mRNA therapeutics.

Abstract Academic libraries are undergoing a profound paradigm shift, evolving from passive hybrid repositories into autonomous, AI-augmented knowledge ecosystems. While traditional hybrid frameworks address basic print-digital coexistence, they suffer from critical vulnerabilities: high-demand resource friction, physical material mutilation, licensing piracy, unauthorized access, and algorithmic bias in digital discovery. This paper introduces a novel operational paradigm—the Zero-Trust Anti-Deviance Architecture (ZT-ADA)—that integrates Generative AI, Predictive Anomaly Detection, and Dynamic Resource Orchestration (DRO). Under ZT-ADA, predictive models anticipate resource surges during peak evaluation cycles, pre-allocating dynamic multi-user digital access and personalized generative summaries to mitigate physical collection stress. Simultaneously, a zero-trust cyber-physical verification matrix continuously evaluates access telemetry to detect physical deviance (mutilation, concealment, retention abuse) and digital breach threats in real time. We present mathematical formulations, operational workflows, risk matrices, and empirical evaluation metrics to establish a resilient, ethical, and scalable blueprint for 21st-century academic libraries.
topics: Library Collection Development and Digital Resources

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in diagnosis, clinical decision support, patient monitoring, and treatment planning, but its integration complicates the allocation of legal responsibility when patients are harmed. This article examines whether the legal frameworks of Türkiye and the European Union adequately protect patients where clinical decisions are shaped by AI systems. Using comparative doctrinal legal analysis, it evaluates professional negligence, institutional duties, product liability, data protection, informed consent, and evidentiary barriers. It argues that physician-centred liability is insufficient when relevant knowledge, control, and preventive capacity are distributed among clinicians, healthcare institutions, technology providers, and regulators. The article develops the Distributed Accountability Framework for AI-Driven Healthcare (DAF-AIH), which maps responsibility across four dimensions—clinical, institutional, technological, and regulatory—and identifies meaningful human oversight, patient-centred transparency, and effective access to evidence as cross-cutting safeguards. The framework does not create automatic collective liability; it offers a structured method for tracing legally relevant duties, control, omissions, and causal contribution. The comparison highlights both the regulatory resources and unresolved remedial gaps in Türkiye and the EU.

documents.abstract: Tax authorities increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) to detect fraudulent refund claims, identity-related fraud, and anomalous financial reporting. This narrative review examines recent research on these methods and the problems that come with deploying them in tax administration. It covers supervised learning, unsupervised anomaly detection, graph neural networks, and privacy-preserving transformer models. It then discusses three groups of challenges: data quality and fragmented fiscal records, the black-box nature of complex models, and the ethical and legal duties of public agencies, including privacy, fairness, and accountability. The reviewed studies show that ML can improve audit selection and surface new fraud patterns, with one study of Italian audits reporting gains of up to 39% in detected evasion. They also show risks: audit selection that ignores race can still produce large racial disparities in the United States, and the Dutch childcare benefits case shows what happens when a risk model is opaque and unchecked. The review concludes that responsible deployment needs explainable models, fairness testing throughout development, privacy protections, and human oversight of final decisions. The article follows no formal search protocol, and future work should test these conclusions with a systematic review.

documents.abstract: Abstract Physiotherapy is moving from an episodic, clinic-centred model of care towards a continuous, data-informed and patient-centred model. Wearable technologies, which include inertial measurement units, surface electromyography sensors, smart textiles, photoplethysmography-based devices, pressure-sensing insoles and smart garments, now capture movement, muscle activity, physiological load and adherence data outside the clinic. When these data streams are interpreted by artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning and deep learning, they can be transformed into clinically meaningful information such as exercise quality, gait deviations, fall risk, fatigue, pain-related behaviour and recovery trajectories. This manuscript reviews the technological foundations of AI-guided wearables, describes their utility across musculoskeletal, neurological, cardiopulmonary, sports, geriatric and paediatric physiotherapy, and explains how they fit within a smart healthcare ecosystem built on the Internet of Medical Things, cloud analytics and tele-rehabilitation. The potential benefits include objective assessment, personalised dosing of exercise, improved adherence, remote supervision, early detection of deterioration and wider access to rehabilitation, particularly for under-served populations. The paper also examines the principal limitations: sensor validity, algorithmic bias, data privacy, regulatory uncertainty, cost, digital literacy and the risk of de-skilling. A five-layer implementation framework and a set of recommendations for clinicians, educators, researchers and policy makers are proposed. It is concluded that AI-guided wearables should be positioned as decision-support tools that extend, and never replace, the clinical reasoning and therapeutic relationship at the centre of physiotherapy practice.

Liver metastasis is a lethal manifestation of diverse malignancies, but its molecular heterogeneity is not readily captured by routine histopathology. Proteomic profiling has identified functional states of metastatic lesions, although their histomorphological and tumor microenvironmental correlates remain incompletely understood. Here, we developed AI-HistoPS, a computational pathology framework for inferring proteomics-informed states from H&E-stained whole slide images. AI-HistoPS integrates pathology foundation model representations with agent-mediated multiple instance learning to capture subtype-associated morphological patterns. Using multicentre cohorts of liver metastases from multiple primary tumor types, we evaluated associations between histomorphology and three proteomic liver metastasis subtypes (LMS1-3). These states were associated with differences in tumor architecture, stromal composition, and immune cell distribution. AI-HistoPS showed subtype discrimination in the discovery cohort and was evaluated across external cohorts, demonstrating the feasibility of histology-derived representations for proteomics-informed stratification across heterogeneous clinical settings. Attention-guided analyses identified tissue regions associated with subtype-related morphological and microenvironmental features. Multiplex immunohistochemistry supported spatial associations between histological patterns and subtype-related protein markers. These findings suggest that routine histopathology may provide a lower-cost approach for approximating proteomics-informed stratification of liver metastases. Further validation in larger, more diverse, prospectively collected cohorts is required before clinical implementation or use in prognostic or treatment-related decision-making.

documents.abstract: Background: Generative AI and large language models are changing how people seek health information, but their effect on maternal health in sub-Saharan Africa is unclear. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on generative AI and maternal health misinformation, examines community health workers (CHWs) as information intermediaries, and proposes a conceptual framework for safe AI implementation. Methods: We ran a purposive search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, ACM Digital Library, and Google Scholar for publications from January 2014 to August 2026. We synthesized findings narratively and used the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) to organize implementation determinants. Results: We found no study of generative AI maternal health misinformation in sub-Saharan Africa. Evidence from high-income settings and non-maternal topics shows AI answers on reproductive health can be inaccurate or inconsistent, and fluent AI text can seem more compelling than human writing. Multi-specialty African benchmarks and a global benchmark review point to a gap between benchmark performance and clinical safety, but maternal-specific performance is unreported. CHWs have a well-documented record of improving maternal and child health, but their ability to identify AI errors is untested. African digital health implementations highlight user-centered design, interoperability, and sustained investment. Conclusions: We propose, as hypotheses for evaluation, localized benchmarking, retrieval-augmented generation restricted to national guidelines with added safeguards, CHW curricula that include AI literacy, and decentralized research hubs. Unvalidated AI could bypass CHW authority and affect trust, though this is unstudied. Priorities include measuring AI use among pregnant women and prospectively evaluating CHW-facing tools.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Urban drainage channels are often inspected only after water-logging has begun, and most low-cost IoT monitors raise a single alert when a water-level threshold is crossed. This paper reviews twenty studies on IoT blockage detection, level-based blockage analysis, ultrasonic sensing, machine learning for sewer systems and AIoT architectures, derives six research gaps from them, and proposes a conceptual AIoT-Based Drainage Blockage Early Warning System (AIoT stands for Artificial Intelligence of Things). The design places two HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensors upstream and downstream of a possible blockage together with a flow input, processes the readings on an ESP32 microcontroller every second, classifies the channel as Normal, Developing Blockage or Severe Blockage, and signals the result locally through green, yellow and red LEDs and a buzzer and remotely through a cloud dashboard. A transparent laboratory channel with a servo-controlled blockage is planned for repeatable testing. The circuit design and a Wokwi simulation are complete, and the estimated hardware cost is about ₹2,300. The contribution is a literature-grounded design and research agenda; the physical prototype and the machine learning classifier have not yet been built or validated.

ALEX: Separation of Decision Authority in an Autonomous Investment System — Deterministic Financial Intelligence, Governed AI, and Automated Trading This technical report presents ALEX, an autonomous investment research and paper-trading platform designed around a fundamental architectural principle: artificial intelligence may assist financial reasoning and explanation without possessing direct authority over automated investment decisions or trade execution. Developed between April and October 2026, ALEX comprises approximately 211,000 lines of production Python code across 307 modules, 1,123 API routes, and approximately 4,000 automated test functions. Unlike architectures that rely on large language models (LLMs) to generate trading decisions, ALEX separates its quantitative investment engine, portfolio management, risk governance, and broker execution into distinct software components. The system incorporates a deterministic five-factor investment scoring model, rule-based portfolio construction, nine reference portfolios, and an execution architecture with 18 pre-trade risk controls. Automated orders are processed through Interactive Brokers in a strictly controlled paper-trading environment. A key architectural property is operational independence from generative AI: the automated fund's decision-to-order path does not require an LLM to select securities, determine portfolio weights, or submit trades. AI is primarily employed for research assistance, financial explanations, education, and conversational interaction. A separate AI-selected model-portfolio feature is explicitly documented as an exception and does not automatically control broker execution. The report includes practical examples of investment scoring, portfolio allocation, risk-based order rejection, financial-statement validation, and system behavior during LLM service interruptions. It also documents the platform's limitations, including incomplete decision reproducibility, data-quality dependencies, parallel quantitative implementations, ongoing security improvements, and the need for longer forward performance evaluation. The principal contribution is an implemented architecture for separating cognitive assistance, investment decision authority, and execution control within an autonomous financial system. ALEX does not claim to have invented algorithmic trading or demonstrated superior investment returns. Instead, it provides a practical engineering case study of how generative AI can be integrated into financial infrastructure without becoming the authoritative component responsible for automated trading decisions. Keywords: Autonomous Investment Systems; Financial Artificial Intelligence; Deterministic Investment Engines; AI Governance; Algorithmic Trading; Decision Authority; Quantitative Finance; Risk Management; Human-Centered AI; Financial Technology. ES: Este Addendum 2026 reúne 20 voces blind (10 Prompt 1 + 10 Prompt 2) de 10 arquitecturas distintas (ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Qwen, Perplexity, Meta AI, Gemini x2, Grok, Kimi K3, Claude) que responden sin leerse entre sí, un año después de Operación Espejo de Verdad (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18012609). documents.abstract: Background Diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) carry risks of recurrence, amputation, and all-cause mortality, but most prediction models address single outcomes and have limited interpretability. We developed an interpretable multi-outcome machine-learning framework for individualised DFU risk assessment and prospective clinical evaluation. Methods We conducted a development and validation study across three hospitals in China from January 1, 2018, to April 30, 2025. We used electronic medical records and follow-up data from 763 patients at Centres A and B to develop and internally validate an ensemble of single-task extreme gradient boosting (ST-XGBoost) and single-task multilayer perceptron (ST-MLP) models to predict cure, recurrence, amputation, and all-cause mortality. The locked ensemble was externally validated in 100 patients at Centre C. Model performance was assessed using discrimination, calibration, and decision curve analysis, with interpretability evaluated using Shapley additive explanations (SHAP). From January 5 to March 5, 2026, we performed a prospective comparative evaluation. We randomised 202 participants (1:1) to usual care or artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted care, of whom 200 were analysed. We compared AI-assisted physician decision-making via an evolvable web-based online prediction platform versus usual care. The outcome was overall quality score of the final clinical recommendation. The platform supports follow-up data collection for future offline model updating. Findings In the training dataset, cure, recurrence, amputation, and all-cause mortality occurred in 638, 208, 226, and 167 patients, respectively; the corresponding numbers in the external validation dataset were 80, 34, 24, and 25. In independent external validation, the ST-XGBoost + ST-MLP ensemble outperformed six comparators, with a macro-averaged AUC of 0.901, accuracy of 0.875, and F1 score of 0.830. Outcome-specific discrimination was highest for amputation (AUC 0.953) and all-cause mortality (AUC 0.951), followed by cure (AUC 0.880) and recurrence (AUC 0.820). In the prospective evaluation, AI-assisted recommendations received higher scores than corresponding clinician recommendations (7.77 vs 6.47; mean difference 1.30, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.08–1.52; p < 0.0001), with the largest gain in completeness. The AI-assisted group showed better short-term follow-up engagement and glucose-management adherence. Interpretation We demonstrate that integrating gradient-boosted trees and neural networks enables explainable prediction of complex DFU trajectories and may support prioritised, individualised clinical decision-making. Nevertheless, recurrence estimates should be interpreted cautiously. Funding Xuzhou Municipal Health Commission Science and Technology Project (XWYHT20240128).

documents.abstract: Accurate prediction of carbon footprint dynamics is essential for climate policy design and sustainable development planning, yet complex nonlinear interactions among energy systems, environmental factors, and socioeconomic activities make estimation challenging. To address this gap, this study proposes an integrated framework combining machine learning, explainable artificial intelligence, and graph neural networks to predict carbon footprints across 27 European countries from 2015 to 2023. Evaluating several algorithms revealed that tree-based models substantially outperformed linear approaches, with LightGBM achieving the highest machine learning performance. SHAP analyses identified fossil fuel dependency, municipal waste generation, environmental impacts, protection capacity, and climate initiatives as the primary predictive determinants. Furthermore, incorporating a country similarity network into Graph Neural Network architectures improved predictive accuracy, with the Graph Attention Network (GAT) delivering the overall best predictive performance. Robustness checks confirmed model stability across various configurations, demonstrating that carbon footprint formation is driven by both national indicators and structural cross-country relationships. Ultimately, this framework bridges a methodological gap in environmental forecasting, offering robust predictive tools for policymakers and actionable, feature-level insights for targeted climate mitigation strategies.

This research explores the potential of Brazilian folklore and literature as a source for audiovisual productions with global reach. Given the growing integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in academic and creative research, this study conducted a comparative analysis of four large language models (ChatGPT-4, Grok-3, DeepSeek v3, and Gemini 2.5). Methodologically, this is an applied, exploratory study with a qualitative approach, based on the collection and triangulation of data artificially generated through a standardized prompt. The results revealed that while the models consistently suggested popular figures such as Saci-Pererê and Iara, a prominent algorithmic bias toward Hollywood commercial patterns and cultural homogenization emerged. DeepSeek v3 showed greater ethnic-cultural diversity by including Indigenous and African myths , but all tools failed to access niche legends or oral traditions. It is concluded that, although AIs are valuable tools for complementing traditional folkloric research, they cannot replace it. In-depth human research remains essential to uncover the nuances and the vast range of lesser-known figures in Brazilian folklore, ensuring the authenticity and originality necessary for cultural and commercial success.
