documents.abstract: Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mengkaji implementasi aplikasi SRIKANDI (Sistem Informasi Kearsipan Dinamis Terintegrasi) terhadap produktivitas tenaga administrasi di Madrasah Aliyah Negeri (MAN) Kota Surabaya. Penelitian menggunakan metode kualitatif deskriptif dengan pengumpulan data melalui wawancara mendalam kepada tiga informan yang dipilih secara purposif berdasarkan representasi pengguna: Kepala Tata Usaha, tenaga administrasi senior, dan pegawai baru. Temuan penelitian memperlihatkan berdasarkan persepsi informan bahwa pemanfaatan aplikasi SRIKANDI berkontribusi dalam peningkatan efisiensi waktu kerja, penghematan biaya operasional, kemudahan dalam memantau kinerja berdasarkan data, serta percepatan penelusuran arsip. Namun demikian, implementasinya masih menghadapi sejumlah kendala yang dikategorikan ke dalam faktor manusia (human factor), faktor teknis (technical factor), dan faktor organisasi (organizational factor). Berdasarkan hasil penelitian tersebut, dapat disimpulkan bahwa keberhasilan transformasi administrasi digital tidak semata-mata ditentukan oleh kualitas teknologi, melainkan juga oleh kesiapan sumber daya manusia dan komitmen organisasi.

Perkembangan large language model (LLM) menimbulkan peluang sekaligus ketergantungan baru terhadap data, model, infrastruktur komputasi, dan mekanisme pengendalian yang berada di luar kendali organisasi atau negara pengguna. Artikel konseptual ini membahas strategi pembangunan kemampuan sovereign AI untuk konteks Indonesia melalui pembangunan dataset lokal dan adaptasi foundation model yang selaras dengan konteks budaya. Kerangka yang diusulkan terdiri atas lima lapisan, yaitu data sovereignty, model adaptation, cultural alignment, evaluation, dan deployment. Dataset lokal diposisikan sebagai aset pengetahuan yang memerlukan provenance, licensing, privacy, access control, dan governance. Adaptasi model memanfaatkan open foundation model melalui continued pre-training atau fine-tuning dengan pendekatan parameter-efficient seperti LoRA. Cultural alignment dirancang melalui preference data dan rubric lokal, sedangkan evaluasi diusulkan mencakup dimensi bahasa, budaya, hukum, safety, dan nilai. Artikel ini menegaskan bahwa sovereign AI tidak identik dengan isolasi teknologi atau pembangunan model dari nol. Kedaulatan dipahami sebagai kemampuan, governance, dan optionality untuk menentukan kapan teknologi global digunakan dan kapan capability yang lebih terkontrol diperlukan. Kerangka ini bersifat konseptual dan memerlukan validasi empiris pada tahap berikutnya. Kata kunci: sovereign AI; dataset lokal; foundation model; cultural alignment; data sovereignty
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is now widely used in academic and daily activities, yet its acceptance may differ across user groups. This study measures the level of AI acceptance among university students and the general public, examines the effect of perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness on behavioral intention, and tests differences between the two groups. A quantitative survey based on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) was conducted with 49 respondents (30 students and 19 members of the public). Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, path analysis, and the Mann–Whitney test. AI acceptance was high (M = 3,60). Perceived ease of use significantly affected perceived usefulness (β = 0,830) and behavioral intention (β = 0,448), whereas the effect of perceived usefulness on behavioral intention was not significant (β = 0,280). Behavioral intention positively affected daily AI use (β = 0,411) but explained only a small share of its variance (R² = 0,169). No significant differences were found between students and the public on any variable. The findings suggest that ease of use is the key to AI adoption, so simple interfaces and user training should be prioritised.

AI tools (ChatGPT, Grammarly, Gemini, QuillBot) are increasingly used in higher education to support learning and writing, but concerns exist about learner dependency and its impact on critical thinking and independent learning. This study examined the association between AI reliance and critical thinking among students from five Kenyan universities. Using a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design, data were collected from 275 students via questionnaires. Quantitative analysis included descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, regression, and ANOVA. Results showed moderate AI reliance for tasks such as assignment preparation and idea generation. A modest positive correlation was found between AI use and critical thinking (r=0.24, p < 0.05). Self-directed learning (β = 0.29) and purposeful AI use (β = 0.21) were significantly associated with critical thinking. ANOVA indicated that moderate AI users had higher critical thinking scores than those reporting low or excessive AI use.

In modern and future telecommunication systems-particularly within 5G-Advanced and emerging 6G networks-data transmission optimization remains a critical challenge in the context of the terahertz (THz) spectrum, ultra-reliable lowlatency communications (URLLC), and massive Internet of Things (mMTC).Analytical models relying on traditional Shannon-Kotelnikov theory fall short in achieving fully efficient resource management and signal recovery under dynamic environments characterized by high fading, multipath propagation, and intense interference.This research provides a comprehensive analysis of the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) algorithms across all stages of data transmission.It proposes a hybrid physicalstatistical framework that merges the mathematical models of the physical layer with data-driven ML methods based on Edge AI.As part of this study, a 5G HetNet topology comprising macrocells, pico-cells, and IoT nodes was simulated using NS-3 (Network Simulator 3).The performance of SVM, Decision Trees, K-means, and PCA was evaluated alongside reinforcement learning models (Q-learning, Deep Q-Networks -DQN).The obtained simulation results demonstrate that the hybrid ML approach, and specifically deep reinforcement learning (RL), enables reducing network latency by up to 22%, increasing overall throughput by 18%, raising the accuracy of anomaly and security attack detection to 94%, and significantly enhancing energy efficiency compared to traditional routing and resource allocation methods.

Abstract: AI is increasingly playing a significant role in sports today, and it's transforming the way athletes are evaluated, trained, and monitored. It enables coaches, sports scientists and athletes to explore vast quantities of performance data and find patterns that they might not otherwise be able to see through traditional methods. Technologies like machine learning, computer vision, wearable technology, predictive analytics, and automated video analysis are also being applied to a growing number of technical skills, physical performance, tactical movements, training workload, recovery and injury risk studies. Such technologies can deliver real-time and personalized data to coaches to create training plans based on the unique requirements of athletes and make informed decisions. AI can also aid in talent identification and performance prediction by integrating data collected from physical, physiological, biomechanical, and psychological factors. While these are advantages, there are also drawbacks to using AI in sports. Data quality, privacy, cost, technical, algorithmic bias and ethical considerations should be taken seriously. The article will explore the key applications of AI in sports performance analysis, as well as its potential benefits in enhancing athlete development and performance, and its current challenges and future prospects.

Introduction and purpose. Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and a leading cause of ischaemic stroke, yet it frequently remains undiagnosed because of its paroxysmal and often asymptomatic nature. Artificial intelligence (AI), and in particular deep learning applied to the electrocardiogram (ECG), has emerged as a transformative approach both for detecting AF when the arrhythmia is present and for predicting future AF from an ECG recorded during sinus rhythm. The purpose of this narrative review is to summarise the current state of knowledge on AI-enabled ECG analysis for the detection and prediction of AF and to critically appraise its clinical readiness. Description of the state of knowledge. Convolutional neural networks can classify AF on single-lead and twelve-lead ECG with cardiologist-level accuracy (area under the curve, AUC, above 0.97 for rhythm classification) and can identify an "electrocardiographic signature" of AF on a normal sinus-rhythm tracing (AUC approximately 0.87). Consumer wearables using photoplethysmography and single-lead ECG achieve pooled sensitivity and specificity around 95%. Predictive models for incident AF reach AUC values of 0.78–0.85 and have been validated prospectively, enriching the diagnostic yield of screening. Nevertheless, false positives, unclassifiable tracings, limited external validity, and the absence of trials demonstrating a reduction in stroke temper enthusiasm. Summary. AI-ECG is a mature and accurate tool for AF detection and a promising instrument for AF prediction, but its translation into improved patient-relevant outcomes remains unproven. Rigorous external validation, outcome-driven randomised trials, and clear regulatory and implementation frameworks are required before routine clinical adoption. Keywords: Atrial Fibrillation; Artificial Intelligence; Deep Learning; Electrocardiography; Mass Screening; Stroke

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping teaching, learning, and research by offering tools that can support educational practice and academic work. This paper examines AI applications in education, their potential benefits, associated challenges, and ethical implications. It considers how AI can assist teachers with lesson planning, instructional materials, assessment, and feedback; support students through personalized learning and explanations of academic concepts; and help researchers with literature searches, data analysis, reference organization, and academic writing. Drawing on a review of existing literature, the paper identifies opportunities to improve educational efficiency, accessibility, and academic productivity. It also highlights concerns involving data privacy, algorithmic bias, inaccurate outputs, academic dishonesty, unequal access to technology, and overdependence on AI tools. The literature points to the importance of user training, ethical guidelines, institutional support, and critical evaluation of AI-generated content (Maphalala & Ajani, 2025; Khatri & Karki, 2023). The paper argues that AI should complement—not replace—teachers, learners, and researchers. Responsible integration requires a balance between technological innovation and human judgment, creativity, critical thinking, and academic integrity.

documents.abstract: Purpose This paper provides evidence on whether corporate investment in artificial intelligence (AI) predicts corporate default risk, using the full term structure of forward-looking probabilities of default (PD). Design/methodology/approach Validated firm-level AI-investment measures built from employee resumes and job postings are merged with NUS-CRI forward-intensity PDs for U.S. listed non-financial firms (outcomes 2011–2018). Because PD is a fraction in [0,1], estimation uses fractional logit with industry and year fixed effects; identification is probed with a university AI-talent-supply instrument in a control-function design with bootstrap inference for the generated regressor, matching and entropy balancing and an extensive robustness battery. Findings A one-standard-deviation increase in AI investment is associated with significantly lower default probability at 12- to 36-month horizons – about 8 basis points at 12 months, roughly one-quarter of the sample mean. The relative effect declines with horizon and is concentrated within the first two years. A control-function test does not reject exogeneity, so the fractional-logit estimates are preferred, with the instrument as corroboration; results are robust to the job-posting measure, alternative industry classifications and screens and R&D and capital-intensity controls. Originality/value To our knowledge, the first firm-level evidence linking validated AI-investment measures to the PD term structure for U.S. listed firms, showing that labor-market footprints of AI adoption carry default-relevant information and that the association is a short-to-medium-horizon phenomenon.

Artificial intelligence can assist audit analysis while changing how professionals evaluate evidence and accept advice. This systematic literature review examines the evidence supporting concerns about over-reliance on AI in audit decision-making. An OpenAlex title-and-abstract search and supplementary Consensus and SciSpace searches conducted on 29 October 2026 identified 149 records. After deduplication and eligibility assessment, 12 empirical journal studies were included. Five experimental reports, five surveys and two qualitative studies were synthesised using a design-sensitive approach and a six-domain critical appraisal. The experimental evidence more clearly demonstrates context-dependent advice-taking and algorithm aversion than the prevalence of inappropriate acceptance of incorrect AI advice. Survey associations between technology use, trust and reported scepticism do not establish behavioural calibration. Qualitative findings identify responsibility and professional learning as consequential organisational concerns. A proposed framework distinguishes output validity, trust, verification, reliance and defensible judgement, and generates four propositions for future testing. Practical implications include access to contradictory evidence, evaluation of both acceptance and rejection errors, and review that examines reasons for reliance. Limited search coverage, inaccessible reports, version differences, partial full-text access and an AI-assisted singleworkflow process constrain confidence. The review supports proportionate safeguards and better behavioural measurement without estimating a population rate of auditor over-reliance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The article examines the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the didactics of Latin, framing AI as a transformative epistemic mediator rather than a mere technological adjunct. In the evolving digital landscape, AI is reshaping educational processes by influencing how knowledge is accessed, structured, and interpreted. The study critically explores four key areas—adaptive learning, gamification, assisted translation, and digital resources—demonstrating how AI can enhance pedagogical personalization, engagement, and inclusive learning experiences. Special attention is given to the challenges posed by algorithmic opacity, teacher mediation, and the ethical tensions surrounding automation in educational settings. The Latin language, understood as a symbolic and logical construct, is presented as uniquely suited to benefit from AI-enhanced learning environments, which can support complex interpretive practices. When implemented within a coherent pedagogical framework, critically and ethically, AI has the potential to revitalize classical language teaching, enhance students’ interpretive skills and metalinguistic skills, foster both critical literacy and meaningful interaction with classical texts. Ultimately, this contribution argues for a humanistic and ethically grounded approach on AI integration in education: Latin and AI together offer new avenues for promoting critical thinking and cultural awareness in education, reaffirming the relevance of classical studies in the digital age. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Inclusion; Teacher Education; Latin Didactics; Inclusive Technologies.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence AI is getting more and more involved in higher education, it is reshaping teaching, learning , assessment, academic administration, research, and even how institutions decide things. In the last few years the fast rise of generative artificial intelligence GenAI, plus intelligent tutoring systems, learning analytics, automated assessment, recommendation systems, and AI assisted administrative tools has opened up new possibilities for universities, yet it also brings worries like academic integrity, data privacy, algorithmic bias, digital inequality, transparency, and changing professional roles. This paper actually uses a secondary-data based systematic review, looking at research and policy sources about AI and digital transformation in higher education. The review brings together outcomes from academic studies, other systematic reviews, and international policy frameworks, sort of to map out the main uses, opportunities, obstacles, and the kind of emerging trends that are starting to show up. What the literature suggests is that AI in education is not only about making content. It also includes adaptive learning, personalized tutoring, intelligent assessment, profiling and prediction, and support for institutional management. At the same time, good adoption does not just happen, it needs institutional policies, AI literacy, ethical safety nets, teacher professional development, careful responsible assessment approaches, and a human centered way of putting things into practice. A number of recent international frameworks stress human agency, ethics, AI competencies, and responsible usage, so there is a clear direction there. Overall the review shows that AI is best understood as augmentation tech with AI to help educators and learners not to flip a switch and replace the educational roles that already exist. For digital transformation a balance must exist, with technical novelty on one side and pedagogical sense together with ethical norms institutional realities and human factors, on the other. None of those should be treated as optional because leaving one out tends to break the system quickly.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Pharmaceutical analysis underpins the identity, purity, potency and safety of medicines. Conventional workflows based on chromatography, spectroscopy and mass spectrometry are reliable but depend on manual interpretation and generate data volumes that are hard to exploit fully. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) offer data-driven tools for peak detection, retention-time and spectral prediction, impurity identification, dissolution and stability modelling, anomaly detection and real-time process analytical technology (PAT). This narrative review, based on a structured search of peer-reviewed and regulatory sources published mainly from 2021 to 2026, compares traditional and AI-enabled workflows, summarises ML methods and their applications across analytical areas, and examines explainable AI, digital twins, generative AI and autonomous laboratories. In the sources reviewed, the strongest evidence concerns spectroscopy-based prediction for PAT and dissolution and retention-time prediction supported by large public datasets, whereas evidence for stability forecasting, rare-impurity identification and autonomous laboratories is limited and seldom validated at industrial scale. Regulatory thinking is converging on risk-based, context-of-use credibility assessment and lifecycle management. We propose a conceptual Intelligent Pharmaceutical Analysis Framework (IPAF) linking instrumentation, data integrity, AI analytics, decision support and governance, and identify priorities: standardised validated datasets, explainable and uncertainty-aware models, and prospective multi-site validation.

The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT) has been advanced as the technical foundation of adaptive, sensor-rich learning environments, yet the structure and maturity of the resulting literature have not been mapped systematically. This study reports a scientometric analysis of 824 Scopus-indexed documents published between 2016 and 2025, retrieved with a TITLE-ABS-KEY query combining AI, IoT, and education and screened in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement. Performance analysis and science mapping were conducted with the bibliometrix R package (Biblioshiny) and VOSviewer, and comprised source, authorship, and country analyses, keyword co-occurrence, a strategic thematic map, thematic evolution across three periods, author co-citation, and a logistic life-cycle model. The corpus was produced by 2,668 authors across 525 sources, and annual output rose from a single document in 2016 to 274 in 2024. Publication is markedly dispersed: computing proceedings series and engineering outlets, rather than education journals, head the Bradford core; conference papers account for 47.1% of research documents; and author productivity departs sharply from Lotka’s law (β = 5.07), with 95.4% of authors contributing a single document. India and China dominate corresponding authorship, whereas international co-authorship remains modest at 20.87%. Artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things, and machine learning form a single central keyword cluster, while educational terms occupy peripheral clusters. The strategic map contains basic and niche themes but no motor theme, and thematic evolution shows continuous lineages for AI and IoT but none for pedagogy. Author co-citation reveals an intellectual base drawn from Industry 4.0, cyber-physical systems, and machine-learning research, with education-specific authors at its periphery. A logistic model signaled saturation (K = 869), but sensitivity analyses showed this to be an artifact of the partial 2025 year; on complete or annualized data, the field is at or just before its inflection point. The field is therefore expanding but unconsolidated, technologically driven, and reliant on an intellectual base imported from outside education. Implications for research agendas, publication strategy, and capacity building are discussed.

Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is one of the most significant technological developments of the 21st century, and it is impacting the global job market in profound ways. AI-powered tools like machine learning, robotics, natural language processing, and automation have transformed the nature of work, the productivity of industries and countries, and the skills that the workforce needs in developed and developing countries. This research paper analyses change in employment, job displacement, skill transformation, productivity increases, wage inequality, and labour market polarization caused by the impact of AI on the global labour market. The study also explores changes in manufacturing, healthcare, financial services, retail, logistics, education and information technology by sector. This study is qualitative and quantitative, based on secondary data obtained from international organizations like the International Labour Organization (ILO), the World Economic Forum (WEF), the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the International Monetary Fund (IMF), and the World Bank (WB). The analysis of the data from 2018 to 2025 will provide insights into the evolving employment landscape as a result of AI adoption. The study highlights the potential of AI to boost productivity, efficiency, and economic growth, as well as the challenges it poses, such as job displacement, technological unemployment, growing income inequality, and skill mismatches. The results indicate that repetitive and routine occupations are most likely to be automated, while creative, emotionally intelligent, and advanced analytical jobs grow. The paper also delves into the new roles in data science, AI engineering, cybersecurity, digital marketing, and human-machine collaboration. The developing countries have different challenges because of poor digital infrastructure, low technological readiness and inadequate training of the workforce. Developed economies, on the other hand, have the better option to adapt via innovation ecosystems and skill development programs. The study emphasizes the importance of governments, educational institutions, multinational corporations, and international organizations to make working life easier for people with disabilities to transition into and out of. The paper argues that AI does not only pose a threat, and is not an automatic assurance of economic well-being, but rather the impact of AI relies on policy response, workforce adaptability and technological ethical governance. Therefore, public policies to promote reskilling and lifelong learning, labour protection, digital inclusion and social security systems are required to ensure the sustainability of employment in the face of technology. The study suggests a collective global governance approach to ensure equitable distribution of the opportunities of AI-enabled economic transformation across societies and labour markets globally. The objectives, as well as the concepts of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Lay of the Land – Labour Market, Employment Trends, Job Displacement, AI's contribution to GDP growth, Workforce Transformation and Digital Skills and Policy recommendations, will be addressed.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality

documents.abstract: Abstract Climate change presents a growing danger to ecosystems, infrastructure, and human safety, heightening the need for prediction systems that are both precise and rapid enough to facilitate prompt decision-making. Artificial intelligence (AI), especially deep learning, has arisen as a revolutionary enhancement to conventional physics-based numerical models. This manuscript examines the application of AI methodologies, such as graph neural networks, transformers, Fourier neural operators, and ensemble deep-learning frameworks, throughout the climate-prediction continuum, encompassing short-term weather forecasting to multi-decadal climate model simulation, sea-level forecasting, and greenhouse gas emission estimation. We encapsulate notable systems documented in contemporary literature, examine the computational and scientific benefits that AI presents in comparison to traditional numerical weather prediction (NWP), and delineate the key obstacles, such as data insufficiency, physical coherence, interpretability, and energy expenditure, that need resolution prior to the reliable implementation of AI-driven climate forecasting at an operational level. We finish with guidance on hybrid physics-AI modelling as a means to get dependable, practical climate insights.

This report presents a literature review and discussion focused on the application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to support future flight operations, particularly within the context of Single Pilot Operations (SPO) and failure mitigation. The scope considered focuses on flight deck operations that support decision-making, reduce pilot workload, and improve situational awareness, with a special emphasis on processes for detecting and reducing the effects of system or aircraft-level failures. Although failure management is a widely studied topic in the aeronautical context (Zolghadri, 2024), there are still few systematic reviews on the specific combination of SPO and AI, even though several isolated studies and reports highlighting the importance of the subject have been published, as discussed in this text.

Abstract For nearly three decades, the National Assessment and Accreditation Council (NAAC) has been India's main mechanism for assuring quality in higher education. Its traditional model — built around a self-reported Self-Study Report, a data validation stage, and an on-site peer-team visit ending in a letter grade — has come under increasing strain. Critics point to slow turnaround, difficulty in standardizing judgments across assessor teams, and the challenge of scaling the process to the thousands of institutions India now wishes to bring under formal quality review. In February 2025, NAAC announced a major reform: a binary accreditation outcome, an optional five-level Maturity-Based Graded Level (MBGL) scale for institutions seeking continuous improvement, a unified national data platform, and the beginnings of an AI-assisted evaluation engine to reduce the burden of manual verification. This paper builds on that reform and proposes, in concrete technical terms, what such an AI-assisted engine could look like. We outline a system that can read and structure Self-Study Reports, cross-check institutional claims against government data sources such as UGC, AICTE, AISHE and NIRF, benchmark institutions against their peers, and present the results to human assessors without replacing their judgment. The discussion is grounded in India's higher-education context: wide variation in digital readiness across institutions, obligations under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and the well-known risk that metric-driven systems can encourage institutions to "write to the metric" rather than improve underlying quality. We conclude with a phased pilot study to test the framework before any wider rollout.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored to overcome the technical and workflow challenges of adaptive radiotherapy (ART) in head and neck cancer (HNC). However, the available evidence remains heterogeneous, with varying degrees of technical and clinical validation. This review evaluated the current role and clinical maturity of AI-enabled ART in HNC. A systematic literature search of PubMed, Scopus and EMBASE was performed from inception to 1 August 2026. Original prospective or retrospective human studies published between 1 January 2020 and 1 August 2026 were eligible. Studies were restricted to photon-based radiotherapy using CBCT, kVCT or MVCT. Eligible studies were classified into four domains: synthetic CT/image enhancement; AI-based auto-segmentation and deformable image registration; anatomical change prediction and adaptive planning; and prediction of ART requirement. Reporting quality was assessed using CLAIM 2024, QUADAS-2 was applied where appropriate. Out of 62 records screened, 25 studies were included. Sixteen studies addressed synthetic CT/image enhancement, seven addressed auto-segmentation/deformable registration, two evaluated anatomical change prediction/adaptive planning, and three investigated predictions of ART requirement, with some overlap between domains. AI consistently demonstrated technical improvements in image quality, CT-number accuracy, segmentation performance and dosimetric agreement. However, evidence for prospective prediction of anatomical change and ART requirement was considerably limited. CLAIM adherence ranged from approximately 68% to 88%, with a mean of 79.9%±5.8%. AI demonstrates substantial technical potential across HNC ART workflows, particularly for image synthesis, segmentation and registration. However, multicentre evidence demonstrating improved clinical decision-making and patient outcomes remains insufficient.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in aquaculture to support monitoring, prediction, automation, and production management, while also creating new requirements for professional competence, ethical oversight, and governance. This systematic literature review, conducted under an integrative approach and reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020, examined practical applications of AI and their implications for professional education and governance in aquaculture. Searches in Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, and Google Scholar identified 877 records, of which 97 met the eligibility criteria and were included in the qualitative synthesis. The evidence was concentrated on technical applications, particularly fish detection and biomass estimation, water and environmental monitoring, automated production systems, health and biosecurity, and feeding and growth optimization. Direct educational evidence was scarce: only one study examined aquaculture professionals' knowledge and interest in AI, and no included study evaluated formal curricular interventions or learning outcomes in Fisheries Engineering. The synthesis also identified concerns involving data quality, algorithmic bias, technological exclusion, privacy, standardization, and accountability. These findings indicate that responsible adoption requires locally representative data, transparent validation, digital and data literacy, human oversight, and coordinated governance. AI has substantial potential to support aquaculture, but its contribution to professional education remains an important and insufficiently investigated research field.

The diagnosis of axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) remains challenging and is frequently delayed. Imaging is central to diagnosis, but relevant inflammatory and structural abnormalities may be subtle, heterogeneous, or overlap with findings related to mechanical stress, anatomical variation, and degeneration. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning, is therefore being investigated to support image interpretation, lesion detection, quantification, and standardized assessment. We synthesize evidence from 12 studies applying convolutional neural networks and related architectures to magnetic resonance imaging and radiographs, automate imaging scores, and combine imaging-derived information with clinical variables. Several models achieved performance comparable to experienced human readers, including during external validation. However, performance may decline in heterogeneous real-world populations for study-specific reasons not explained solely by scanner or protocol differences. No AI tool currently has regulatory clearance for autonomous use in axSpA, and applications remain largely confined to research and clinical trials.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This review measured how often, and in what context, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) refers to artificial intelligence (AI), including generative AI, in warning letters. A search was conducted of the full text of all FDA warning letters issued from January 1, 2022, through September 28, 2026, taken from FDA’s public warning letter database. The search terms were “artificial intelligence,” “AI,” “machine learning,” and 4 related terms. Every letter containing a term was assessed and read in full, and the violations cited in each included letter were counted. Form FDA 483s and establishment inspection reports (EIRs) that refer to AI were described separately. Of 3,011 warning letters, 7 (0.23%) referred to AI: 3 device, 3 tobacco, and 1 drug letter. Only the April 2026 letter to Purolea Cosmetics Lab treated a firm’s use of AI as a violation, citing unreviewed AI-generated documents under 21 CFR 211.22(c). In addition, 1 EIR and 2 Form 483s referred to AI. FDA references to AI in warning letters are rare, recent, and heterogeneous, and most describe AI-enabled products subject to existing authorization requirements. The Purolea letter shows that FDA will cite unreviewed AI output under existing current good manufacturing practice (CGMP) rules.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Increasingly, Artificial Intelligence (AI) is influencing the way courts operate. However, there are significant differences regarding the integration and regulation of the use of AI in various jurisdictions. While most studies have thus far concentrated mainly on issues related to ethics and country-specific national AI strategies, existing literature has paid relatively little attention to what regulatory conditions must exist prior to and subsequent to the introduction of AI technology within the court system. This article examines regulatory preparedness and accountability in a comparative analysis of Indonesia, Singapore and Uganda. These three countries are at significantly varying levels of digitalization in their judicial processes. Using both a doctrine-based and comparative method, this article assesses legislative and policy frameworks, institutional capabilities, digital infrastructure, judicial oversight, transparency, explanations and procedural protections. The study contributes to judicial AI governance scholarship by showing, through a comparative analysis, that judicial digitalisation alone does not establish regulatory readiness for AI and that regulatory readiness and accountability must develop together rather than in sequence. An effective AI-enabled justice governance system requires appropriate legal and institutional frameworks that protect judicial independence, procedural fairness, and meaningful human oversight, while also allowing for technologically innovative solutions that are consistent with the rule of law.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as an important technology for developing smart cities by improving urban services, resource management, public transportation, energy efficiency, environmental monitoring, and citizen services. The increasing population of urban areas creates challenges related to traffic congestion, pollution, waste management, electricity consumption, and efficient public administration. Traditional city management systems often depend on manual monitoring and separate information systems, which can limit real-time decision-making and coordination. This paper presents a structured review of AI applications in smart cities and proposes an integrated AI-based framework for intelligent urban management. The proposed framework combines the Internet of Things (IoT), machine learning, data analytics, cloud computing, and intelligent decision-support mechanisms to collect, process, and analyze urban data. It focuses on traffic management, smart energy systems, waste collection, environmental monitoring, and citizen services. The paper also discusses the benefits, implementation challenges, limitations, and future research opportunities associated with AI-enabled urban development. Existing research indicates that AI can support more efficient and responsive city services; however, data privacy, cybersecurity, infrastructure costs, interoperability, algorithmic bias, and digital inclusion remain important concerns. The proposed framework provides a conceptual foundation for developing sustainable, intelligent, and citizen-centered smart cities.

Artificial intelligence (AI) adoption in schools creates opportunities for instructional innovation but also raises questions concerning governance, professional judgement, and institutional readiness. This study examined AI integration and governance in selected United Arab Emirates (UAE) schools and developed a leadership-guided implementation framework. An exploratory sequential mixed-methods design combined semi-structured interviews with 10 purposively selected teachers and school leaders and a subsequent structured survey of 80 respondents, selected through stratified sampling. Interview transcripts underwent thematic analysis; quantitative responses were analysed using weighted means, standard deviations, and Pearson product–moment correlations at the .05 significance level. Seven qualitative themes clustered into AI integration and AI governance. Overall AI integration was rated moderate (grand weighted mean [GWM] = 3.41), with adaptive integration highest (3.76), followed by professional productivity (3.38) and AI-enhanced teaching (3.08). Overall AI governance was high (GWM = 3.32), led by ethical governance (3.66), followed by strategic governance (3.34), organisational support (3.34), and uneven governance (2.97). Organisational support was significantly associated with all three AI-integration dimensions, while adaptive integration had its strongest observed association with ethical governance (r = .539, p < .001). Integrated findings informed the proposed Leadership-Guided AI Integration and Governance Framework for UAE Schools, emphasising pedagogical use, human oversight, ethical safeguards, strategic leadership, professional learning, and institutional readiness. The proposed framework is a study-derived practical output, not a causally validated model.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) within telemedicine has revolutionized virtual healthcare delivery by enabling high-precision diagnostics and tailored treatment strategies remotely. This paper evaluates state-of-the-art AI models applied to medical imaging and clinical text data within telehealth platforms, highlighting significant improvements in diagnostic accuracy and clinical decision support. Using deep learning architectures like ResNet-50 for imaging and BERT for natural language processing of electronic health records, the framework demonstrates enhanced patient care personalization and operational efficiency. Survey feedback from clinicians and patients underscores AI's practical benefits in improving healthcare accessibility and quality in remote settings. Challenges, including algorithmic biases and data privacy risks, are discussed, along with future research directions aimed at sustaining AI-driven telemedicine enhancements to health systems worldwide.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Introduction: Feedback is central to medical education, and generative artificial intelligence (AI) has made individualized, timely, and scalable feedback possible. Questions remain, however, about its accuracy, contextual relevance, and capacity to promote learning compared with feedback from faculty and clinical supervisors. Objective: To analyze the evidence on AI-generated feedback compared with human feedback in medical education, considering its quality, educational effectiveness, applicability, and limitations. Methods: Integrative review structured with the PICo strategy. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and LILACS were searched for studies published between January 2020 and October 2026 in English, Portuguese, or Spanish. Studies were classified by level of evidence, and findings were synthesized through interpretive thematic analysis. Results: Eleven studies from Canada, the United States, Germany, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Japan were included: five randomized trials (level II) and six comparative descriptive or mixed-methods studies (level VI). AI-generated feedback generally matched or exceeded human feedback in comprehensiveness, consistency, and adherence to predefined criteria, especially in written, structured, and simulated tasks. Human feedback was superior in clarity, relevance, and accuracy in some studies and in more complex diagnostic and therapeutic situations. Learning outcomes were measured only in the short term, and hybrid models combining AI data with faculty input showed favorable results. Conclusion: AI can increase the availability and consistency of feedback but does not replace the clinical and pedagogical judgment of faculty. Supervised integration of both modalities is the most consistent approach, and studies with longer-term outcomes and Latin American settings are needed.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Web-based learning environments has transformed teaching, learning, assessment, and information sharing in higher education. Artificial Intelligence (AI) supports personalized learning, automated assessment, intelligent tutoring, and educational data analysis. At the same time, the increasing dependence on digital platforms creates cybersecurity challenges, including computer viruses, malicious software, unauthorized access, data breaches, identity theft, and misuse of personal information. Students, teachers, librarians, researchers, and educational administrators increasingly depend on learning management systems, cloud-based resources, digital libraries, and online assessment platforms. Protecting these systems and the information they contain has therefore become an important responsibility for educational institutions. artificial intelligence, computer viruses, and data protection in web-based learning environments. It discusses the potential of AI to improve cybersecurity monitoring, identify suspicious activities, detect unusual access patterns, and support the protection of educational information. It also considers the risks associated with AI-enabled attacks, inaccurate automated decisions, privacy violations, and excessive collection of student data. The paper adopts a descriptive and analytical approach based on a review of relevant literature, cybersecurity frameworks, and data-protection principles. It proposes an integrated approach involving secure system design, regular software updates, access control, encryption, user awareness, responsible AI governance, and institutional cybersecurity policies. The paper concludes that secure and ethical digital education requires cooperation among technology providers, educational institutions, teachers, librarians, students, and policymakers.

This study examines the extent to which generative artificial intelligence tools (ChatGPT, Gemini, and DeepSeek) can generate middle school geometry questions aligned with the cognitive levels of Bloom’s Revised Taxonomy. The study also evaluates the quality and taxonomic appropriateness of these questions based on expert judgments. A convergent parallel mixed-methods design was employed. A total of 30 geometry questions, including open-ended and multiple-choice items, were generated by the AI tools using structured prompts. Ten mathematics education experts evaluated each question using a rubric that assessed alignment with the intended Bloom level. Quantitative data were analyzed using frequencies, percentages, and Gwet’s AC1 agreement coefficient, while qualitative data were analyzed through thematic content analysis to identify patterns in expert justifications. The findings indicate that all three AI tools perform relatively well at lower and middle cognitive levels (understanding, applying, and analyzing), whereas their performance declines at higher levels (evaluating and creating). DeepSeek and Gemini showed higher overall alignment with targeted cognitive levels compared to ChatGPT. However, expert agreement decreased significantly at higher-order levels, indicating inconsistencies in how these levels are interpreted and represented. Qualitative findings revealed issues related to insufficient cognitive depth, weak distractors in multiple-choice items, and mismatches between intended and actual cognitive levels. Overall, the results highlight both the potential and limitations of generative AI in educational assessment and emphasize the necessity of expert supervision in ensuring pedagogical and taxonomic accuracy.This study compares the performance of three generative artificial intelligence tools—ChatGPT, Gemini, and DeepSeek—in generating questions aligned with Bloom’s six cognitive levels in middle school geometry. The participants consisted of ten mathematics teachers with expertise in mathematics education. The teachers evaluated the AI-generated questions for alignment with the intended cognitive level and provided judgments on their taxonomic appropriateness and overall quality. Quantitative analyses examined the agreement between the intended cognitive level and the levels assigned by participants. In addition, qualitative content analysis was used to analyze participants’ evaluations and comments. The findings highlight both the potential and limitations of generative AI tools and emphasize the importance of expert supervision in AI-supported assessment practices.

Predicting urban energy consumption (EC) under digitalization and artificial intelligence (D&AI) remains challenging because feature interactions obscure input–output relationships. Using data from 275 Chinese cities, this study integrates the Decision Deep and Cross Feature Transformation Network (DDCFTN) with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). DDCFTN combines deep and cross networks, decision-tree-based feature processing, and feature transformation to capture higher-order interactions and nonlinearities. It outperforms evaluated baselines, achieving test-set RMSE, MAE, and R 2 values of 18,360.16, 12,915.71, and 0.97. Nadeau-Bengio corrected paired t-tests with Holm adjustment confirm significant improvements across all metrics, with robustness across seeds, target specifications, regional subsets, and city-grouped ten-fold cross-validation (mean R 2 = 0.89). Six D&AI variables rank among the ten most important predictors; DIF contributes 6.75% of total SHAP importance. DIF interactions are heterogeneous and nonlinear, sometimes reversing from negative to positive contributions. City-level out-of-sample sensitivity analyses broadly corroborate these patterns and indicate possible turning points, supporting city-specific energy policies.

Purpose: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is increasingly used to reduce hallucination in medical large language models (LLMs), but authentic retrieval does not necessarily ensure clinically correct output. We evaluated whether full-text-enriched RAG improves the clinical reliability of locally deployed models for perioperative inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) question answering. Methods: We constructed a locally deployed full-text IBD perioperative knowledge base and a 50-question high-difficulty benchmark. Two 8B models (Qwen3-VL-8B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B) were evaluated under matched no-retrieval and RAG conditions. Three physicians independently scored clinical accuracy, patient safety, and faithfulness under a source-blinded, format-homogeneous protocol. Evidence traceability was assessed objectively by verifying all retrieved PubMed identifiers (PMIDs) against PubMed. Results: All retrieved PMIDs existed in PubMed (236 verifications; 187 unique), confirming source-existence authenticity at the retrieval layer. RAG significantly improved Qwen3 accuracy (Δ=+0.44, P< 0.001) but not DeepSeek accuracy (Δ=+0.21, P=0.09), and the model-by-retrieval interaction for accuracy was not significant. Patient safety showed no reliable benefit. Faithfulness decreased significantly with RAG on Qwen3 (Δ=− 0.24, P< 0.001), with a significant model-by-retrieval interaction. Inter-rater reliability was excellent (ICC 0.86– 0.93). Conclusion: PubMed-based retrieval achieved source-existence authenticity but did not consistently improve clinical correctness or safety. Authentic references could accompany incorrect or unsafe conclusions, indicating that evidence traceability and clinical reliability should be evaluated separately. Additional model-external safety mechanisms may be warranted in high-risk settings but require independent validation. Keywords: retrieval-augmented generation, RAG, large language models, LLMs, hallucination, inflammatory bowel disease, IBD, perioperative medicine, patient safety, on-premises deployment
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enables language models to answer enterprise questions using external documents; however semantic retrieval and multi-agent delegation create authorization risks when access checks occur only after search or answer generation. This study presents a literature-informed architecture for authorization-aware multi-agent RAG in which a policy decision point evaluates current user and resource attributes, whereas a policy enforcement point restricts the eligible candidate set before content reaches rerankers, agents, or a large language model. This design combines role-based and attribute-based access control, semantic embeddings, vector search, least-privilege delegation, provenance-aware auditing, and policy revalidation at protected access boundaries. A focused survey identifies risks including semantic overfetch, cross-domain synthesis leakage, stale permissions, and delegation escalation. The paper defines authorization-correctness conditions and proposes an evaluation protocol that compares authorization-first retrieval with a retrieve-then-filter baseline. The metrics include unauthorized-context exposure, authorized Recall@k, answer relevance, latency, revocation propagation time, delegation violations, and audit completeness. This study is a survey and design contribution; no benchmark results are claimed because the proposed prototype has not yet been empirically evaluated.

Joining unfamiliar software projects forces developers to spend days deciphering complex codebases, API routes, and runtime flows. Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines should help, but they break down on source code in practice. New engineers rarely know what specific questions to ask, and standard chunking blindly slices code mid-function. To solve these issues without manual intervention, we present RepoInsight, an end-to-end system that automatically generates an 11-facet architectural report directly from a GitHub repository URL without requiring human queries. To preserve enclosing syntax without inflating prompt token volume, RepoInsight implements hierarchical parent-child retrieval: granular 500-character child chunks are embedded via Cohere (384 dimensions) and indexed in PostgreSQL pgvector, while complete parent source files are retrieved dynamically through single batched relational queries. To control inference latency and avoid rate limits, the system applies order-preserving file deduplication to consolidate 11 architectural facets into 7 batched prompts. Generation routes through a three-tier fallback hierarchy (Groq -> Gemini 1.5 Flash -> Cohere Command-R) paired with regular-expression JSON sanitization. Empirical evaluations across seven benchmark repositories show that RepoInsight reduces redundant prompt tokens by an average of 40.2%, accelerates nearest-neighbor vector retrieval by 16.1x via HNSW graph indexing, and achieves 100% request completion under severe upstream throttling where single-provider baselines crash on 63.6% of queries. This architecture offers a practical, high-throughput foundation for automated developer onboarding. Github : geethika1207/RepoInsight-Backend: AI-powered GitHub repository intelligence engine built with FastAPI, PostgreSQL, pgvector, and LLMs. Clone any public repository, generate semantic embeddings, and chat with your codebase using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).

Abstract. This scientific article examines the major organizational, institutional, technological, and human factors that hinder the implementation of Agile management in tax authorities and analyzes possible approaches to overcoming these barriers. In the context of accelerating digital transformation and public sector modernization, tax authorities are increasingly required to develop flexible, responsive, transparent, and citizen-oriented management systems. From this perspective, Agile management represents a promising managerial approach that can improve decision-making speed, strengthen cooperation among employees and departments, enhance the quality of public services, and increase the ability of tax authorities to respond effectively to changing economic, technological, and regulatory conditions. The article focuses particular attention on bureaucratic organizational structures, resistance to organizational change, limited employee autonomy, insufficient digital competencies, inadequate technological infrastructure, weak cross-functional cooperation, and the lack of an Agile-oriented organizational culture. Furthermore, practical measures for overcoming these barriers are proposed, including strong managerial support, continuous professional development, gradual implementation of Agile principles, improvement of digital infrastructure, development of cross-functional teams, and enhancement of internal communication mechanisms. The study concludes that the systematic adaptation of Agile management principles to tax administration can contribute to greater organizational efficiency, improved service quality, increased employee engagement, and enhanced institutional flexibility. The findings provide a theoretical and practical basis for modernizing tax administration through Agile-oriented management approaches. Keywords: Agile management, tax authorities, digital transformation, organizational change, bureaucracy, employee autonomy, tax administration, public sector.

Student engagement positively influences academic achievement, yet instruments suited to the Indonesian cultural context remain limited. This study aimed to develop a valid, reliable, and user-friendly student engagement scale for high school students. Using a quantitative descriptive design, the study involved 295 male and female students aged 15–18 years recruited through convenience sampling. The scale comprised three dimensions: behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement. The results showed that the scale demonstrated a good model fit based on the goodness-of-fit indices (χ2/df = 1.60; CFI = 0.966; TLI = 0.962; SRMR = 0.074; RMSEA = 0.045) and good reliability, with Cronbach’s alpha values of 0.844 for emotional engagement, 0.753 for behavioral engagement, and 0.782 for cognitive engagement. The developed scale can be used by teachers, counselors, and educational researchers to identify students’ levels of engagement and inform the development of programs to improve student engagement.

AI-supported English speaking offers opportunities for rehearsal and feedback, yet the relationship between perceived AI usefulness and learners’ self-perceived communicative competence remains insufficiently understood. This cross-sectional study examined associations among perceived usefulness, intrinsic motivation, higher-order engagement, deep and surface learning, and self-perceived communicative competence. Survey data from 420 Vietnamese undergraduate and postgraduate students with experience in AI-supported English speaking were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling. Engagement was conceptualised as a reflective higher-order construct comprising behavioural, cognitive, and agentic dimensions. The findings revealed positive associations between perceived usefulness and intrinsic motivation, as well as between intrinsic motivation and engagement. Engagement was positively associated with deep learning and self-perceived communicative competence (β = .460), but negatively associated with surface learning. Deep and surface learning also showed significant associations with communicative self-perceptions in opposite directions, although their direct associations were weaker than that of engagement. The model explained 35.0% of the variance in self-perceived communicative competence, rather than objectively assessed speaking proficiency. These findings highlight the importance of purposeful interaction, critical evaluation of AI feedback, and learner-initiated clarification in fostering meaningful English-speaking practice beyond AI use alone. Longitudinal studies incorporating direct speaking assessments are needed to determine whether these associations extend to actual communicative performance.

The rapid adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming the accounting profession, creating opportunities for enhanced efficiency while raising concerns regarding employees’ adaptability, job security, and long-term engagement. This conceptual study proposes an integrated framework for examining Sustainable Employee Engagement (SEE) among accounting professionals in Malaysia. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory (SDT), the framework investigates AI adoption, perceived organizational support, and job security as key technological and organizational factors influencing SEE through the mediating role of technology self-efficacy. SEE extends conventional employee engagement by emphasizing employees’ capacity to sustain physical, cognitive, emotional, and behavioural involvement while maintaining adaptability, well-being, and professional relevance during continuous technological transformation. The proposed framework suggests that supportive organizational conditions, employment stability, and effective AI adoption strengthen employees’ confidence in learning, using, and adapting to emerging technologies, thereby fostering sustainable engagement. The study contributes to the literature by positioning technology self-efficacy as a psychological mechanism linking technological and organizational conditions with SEE. Practically, the framework provides guidance for accounting firms and HRD practitioners in developing training, digital upskilling, organizational support, and talent management strategies that promote a resilient, adaptable, and sustainably engaged accounting workforce in AI-enabled workplaces.

Road agencies are investing in artificial intelligence to inspect pavements, forecast deterioration and plan maintenance, yet the value of these tools ultimately depends on whether they improve the interventions that are funded and delivered. This critical narrative review examines the gap between predictive performance and intervention quality in pavement maintenance, termed here the artificial intelligence intervention gap. Literature was identified through structured searches of multidisciplinary and regional scholarly indexes, supplemented by citation tracking and institutional sources, and was appraised for design adequacy, validation practice, causal identification and decision relevance. The synthesis is organised along a decision chain that runs from sensing and condition assessment, through deterioration prediction and estimation of treatment effects, to optimisation, implementation and outcome feedback. The evidence is strongest for automated distress detection and short-term condition prediction, where deep learning and ensemble models frequently achieve high accuracy on benchmark or single-agency data. Confidence weakens progressively along the chain. Performance claims rarely survive transfer across regions, survey technologies or time periods, validation designs often ignore spatial and temporal dependence, and explanations derived from post hoc attribution methods are commonly interpreted as causal mechanisms. Treatment effects are usually inferred from observational records in which maintenance was assigned according to condition, so selection bias and endogeneity remain largely unaddressed outside a small econometric and causal-inference literature. Reinforcement learning and metaheuristic planning studies report cost savings, but most are trained and evaluated within simulators built from the same associational models, and few compare recommended policies with realised outcomes. Implementation evidence, including digital twins and language-model assistants, is at an early, largely demonstrative stage. The review argues that pavement maintenance requires an evidence-based decision-making standard in which intervention effects are explicitly identified, uncertainty is propagated into decisions, decision quality rather than prediction error is the primary evaluation criterion, and agencies monitor the outcomes of recommended treatments. Priorities include benchmark datasets with recorded interventions, quasi-experimental and pragmatic field evaluations of treatments, decision-focused model training and prospective comparison of algorithmic and conventional programmes.

This systematic review comprehensively explores the multi-dimensional application mechanism, practical optimization effects and current research status of user-centered design (UCD) in residential wardrobe innovation. Guided by the PRISMA framework, this study adopts a rigorous systematic literature review methodology to ensure the standardization and transparency of the screening and synthesis process. Relevant literature covering wardrobe design, user-centered design, furniture usability and residential user experience was retrieved from the Web of Science and Scopus databases. Following strict screening based on unified inclusion and exclusion criteria, 48 peer-reviewed academic studies were finally selected for thematic coding and systematic synthesis. A standardized coding matrix was developed to extract core variables, including UCD dimensional characteristics, wardrobe functional and experiential performance, user adaptive effects and scenario-based boundary conditions. This review clarifies that UCD improves wardrobe comprehensive performance through three hierarchical pathways: physiological ergonomic adaptation, precise functional demand matching, and multi-scenario experience upgrading. The optimization effects of UCD exhibit prominent dual heterogeneity across user groups and residential usage scenarios. Design iteration, intelligent technology embedding and spatial environmental characteristics serve as critical moderating factors affecting UCD design outcomes. This review systematically sorts out existing research contradictions (cost limitation vs. long-term value optimization) and theoretical gaps in dimensional differentiation and boundary mechanism research. The findings provide practical guidance on humanized, inclusive and scenario-adaptive wardrobe design; while enriching the practical application of human-factor engineering theory, user experience theory and inclusive design theory in residential furniture innovation.

documents.abstract: Background: Burnout among resident doctors is increasingly recognised as a major occupational health concern due to prolonged working hours, academic burden, sleep deprivation, and emotional stress. Burnout adversely affects psychological well-being, clinical performance, and quality of patient care. The present study was conducted to assess burnout and its correlates among resident doctors in a tertiary care teaching hospital of Meerut. Material & Methods: A hospital-based cross-sectional study was conducted among 262 resident doctors working in a tertiary care teaching hospital in Meerut, Uttar Pradesh, from November 2024 to November 2025. Participants were selected using purposive sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire comprising sociodemographic and residency-related variables along with validated scales, including the Copenhagen Burnout Inventory (CBI), Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-4), Brief Emotional Intelligence Scale (BEIS-10), and FACIT Spiritual Well-Being Scale. Data were analysed using SYSTAT version 13.2. Chi-square test and logistic regression analysis were applied. A p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results: Among the 262 resident doctors, Overall burnout was moderate to high in 50% residents. Moderate-to-high perceived stress was present among 83.7% residents. Most participants had moderate emotional intelligence (52.3%) and moderate-to-high spiritual well-being (85.5%). Long duty hours, frequent night duties, and high perceived stress showed a significant association with burnout. Conclusion: Half of the participants had moderate-to-high burnout, while 13.0% had high burnoutPerceived stress and emotional intelligence were independently associated with high burnout in the adjusted model.

Numerous primary school students reveal low learning motivation in social studies because the material is abstract and less relevant to their lives. An innovative learning model that integrates local cultural values is needed to make learning more interesting and meaningful. This study aims to test the effectiveness of a social studies learning model that contains character values of the local wisdom tradition in increasing the learning motivation of elementary students. Local wisdom from Sumatra has values of togetherness, unity, and collective spirit that can be integrated into character education. The study used a quasi-experimental design with a post-test-only control group design model involving three fourth-grade classes, consisting of two experimental classes and one control class. Data were collected through a learning motivation questionnaire based on cognitive motivation theory and analyzed using one-way ANOVA and the LSD post hoc test. The results reveal a significant difference in learning motivation between groups, with the highest score shown by the class that received learning based on local wisdom character values. This finding indicates that the integration of local cultural values in social studies learning is effective in building students' intrinsic motivation. This model is an innovative alternative in developing character education that is contextual and relevant to students' cultural backgrounds.

This paper argues that the central problem posed by contemporary artificial intelligence is not whether computational systems can reproduce the observable functions of human cognition, but whether their expanding integration into social institutions encourages a reduction of human judgment, creativity, and collective autonomy to measurable and optimizable processes. I address Geoffrey Hinton’s assertion that AI models can obtain consciousness as a starting point for a further investigation of digital barbarism, the trend to imaginatively personify digital applications. Drawing on Thomas Nagel's account of subjective experience and Cornelius Castoriadis' theory of the social imaginary, I develop a critique of algorithmic reductionism that distinguishes the phenomenological limits of computational explanations from the political consequences of deploying AI within corporate and technocratic institutions. I argue that the democratic challenge of AI lies in preserving the capacity of individuals and communities to create new social significations, deliberate about collective ends, and determine the institutional conditions of their technological lives

documents.abstract: Sericulture provides an important source of livelihood for many rural and tribal households in India. However, farmers engaged in sericulture often face occupational health risks, limited access to improved tools, weak value addition, and poor market linkages. To address these constraints, five capacity-building programmes were organised under the ICAR–Tribal Sub-Plan (TSP) project in Udham Singh Nagar district of Uttarakhand. A total of 280 beneficiaries participated across the five programmes, with programme-specific enrolment of 80 in occupational health training (T1), 60 in ergonomic-tool training (T2), 50 in value-added product training (T3), 60 in visual merchandising training (T4), and 30 in cocoon-product exhibition and marketing (T5). Training was delivered at village and university settings through lectures, demonstrations, hands-on activities, and market exposure. Outcomes were evaluated using the participant group relevant to each training module rather than the aggregate total of 280. In T1, the mean knowledge score increased from 38.6% before training to 83.4% after training, a 44.8 percentage-point increase. Among T2 participants, adoption of at least one ergonomic tool increased from 13.3% at baseline to 68.3% at the three-month follow-up. Among T3 participants, 76.0% produced saleable value-added products after training. Participants also expressed high satisfaction, with an overall mean score of 4.62 out of 5.00. The findings indicate programme-associated improvements in occupational-safety knowledge, technology adoption, vocational skills, and marketing exposure, while the programme-specific denominators should be considered when interpreting these outcomes.

documents.abstract: ISSUE ADDRESSED: Although volunteering has been linked to well-being, little is known about the mechanisms underpinning these associations. This study sought to understand the conditions under which benefits occur for older adults who volunteer. METHODS: A community-based sample of 458 participants was recruited for this cross-sectional survey through online study advertisements via social media, email and newsletters. The primary predictor variables were the 21 domains of Work Design Characteristics, and the secondary predictor was Physical Functioning. Outcomes included the Scale of Positive and Negative Experiences, the Satisfaction with Life Scale and the Flourishing Scale. RESULTS: Findings showed social support and favourable work conditions were associated with higher life satisfaction and psychological flourishing, while interactions outside the organization were linked to negative affect. Task characteristics (e.g., variety of tasks) and knowledge characteristics (e.g., skills required) were more strongly associated with higher well-being among volunteers with poorer physical functioning. CONCLUSIONS: This study extends current understanding of the contextual, psychological and subjective factors influencing the relationship between volunteering and well-being in later life. The findings highlight that specific aspects of the volunteer experience are differentially associated with well-being, especially for those with poorer functional health. SO WHAT?: These findings have direct implications for volunteer organizations seeking to design roles that maximize well-being benefits for older adults. Given the rapid ageing of the global population and increasing reliance on volunteer contributions, this research area is essential for informing policies and practices that support older adults' engagement in fulfilling and sustainable volunteer roles.

Large language models now write clinical summaries: discharge summaries, emergency department encounter summaries, progress note summaries, referral letters and clinic visit summaries. Each summary is read, trusted and signed by a clinician, and errors in it travel into the record. This systematic review and meta-analysis asked a single question with a per-summary denominator: in studies that checked LLM-generated clinical summaries against the source record, a clinician-written summary, or blinded expert rating, what proportion of summaries contained at least one clinically significant error? Studies were searched from 2022 to 2026 across PubMed, Europe PMC (including its preprint index), Semantic Scholar and ClinicalTrials.gov, all run on 31 October 2026, with backward citation chasing of the included studies. Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, CENTRAL, IEEE Xplore and the ACM Digital Library were not run; OpenAlex was blocked by a provider rate limit and was not searched. Screening and extraction were each done twice independently, with every disagreement settled by reading the source. Risk of bias used a modified QUADAS-2 tool with QUADAS-AI signalling questions, specified before extraction. Proportions were pooled with a random-effects generalised linear mixed model (logit link), with tau squared, I squared and a prediction interval reported. The search found 991 records; 483 were screened after deduplication, 48 reports were assessed in full, and 11 studies (22 arms, 21 LLM and 1 human) were included. The primary outcome could not be pooled: only 1 of the 11 studies reported the proportion of summaries with at least one clinically significant error (13 of 62 summaries, 21.0 percent, exact 95 percent CI 11.7 to 33.2), and of the 48 reports assessed in full, 31 (65 percent) reported no extractable per-summary error count at all. A supplementary pool of summaries with at least one error of any audited type (post hoc, Amendment 01) gave 60.6 percent (95 percent CI 29.8 to 84.7; 5 units, 4 studies, 323 summaries; prediction interval 6.9 to 97.0). By error type, 20.7 percent of summaries had at least one omission (16 units, 1011 summaries), 17.6 percent had at least one fabrication or addition (8 units, 1226 summaries; a pool the paper warns is close to uninterpretable as a single frequency), and 27.9 percent had at least one inaccuracy (5 units, 500 summaries). One study rated 1 of 100 summaries as likely to cause moderate harm. No study reported matched LLM and human error counts, so that comparison could not be fitted. Certainty was rated very low for every rateable outcome (GRADE), and the LLM versus human comparison was not rateable. The package contains the manuscript (PDF and Markdown), the screening and extraction datasets, risk of bias assessments and the analysis datasets. Analysis code is in the linked GitHub repository. The work was carried out by an LLM research team under a single accountable human author; the team log, prompts and adjudication records are in the repository. Registration: no PROSPERO number was issued for this review. The protocol, timestamped before screening, is published inside the linked GitHub repository.
